bottlenecks.name: Aerothermal environment: laminar-turbulent transition, shock-boundary-layer interaction (SBLI), gap and cavity heating
bottlenecks.description: Predicting where the boundary layer turns turbulent and how much heat shock interactions (flaps, hinge lines, tile steps and gaps) deposit. Turbulent heating runs roughly 3-5x laminar (general), so unpredictable transition forces designers to assume early or fully turbulent flow. RANS models fail on hypersonic SBLI: they mispredict separation and the joint heat-flux/shear signature (Raje et al., arXiv 2412.13985 v2, Apr 2025). Predicting transition on complex 3D geometry is still the subject of a coordinated international effort (AIAA virtual collection, Mar 2026), and BOLT-1B (Mach 7.2) confirmed that flight transition behaves differently from wind-tunnel transition (JHU APL, Jan 2026).
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Mixed. Solved in principle but expert-scarce: 3D linear and nonlinear stability analysis (PSE, plane-marching PSE, resolvent/input-output), setup of wall-modeled LES and DNS, gap-heating analysis. A few specialist groups worldwide do these, taking months per vehicle; an on-demand AI unlock (P1) would make them routine by 2027-28 in S2. Genuinely open: receptivity to the flight disturbance environment, transition induced by roughness or ablation, and non-Boussinesq SBLI heat-flux closures. AI can propose theory for these, but flight and quiet-tunnel data gate validation.

bottlenecks.name: Thermochemical nonequilibrium and radiative heating (Mars/Venus CO2 entries, Earth return at 11-14 km/s)
bottlenecks.description: Shock-layer chemistry and radiation set the heating for fast entries. For the 8 km/s Mars Sample Retrieval Lander (SRL) entry, radiation exceeded the convective heating of MSL. Baseline models under-predicted vacuum-ultraviolet (VUV) emission by up to 2x against NASA's EAST shock tube, and three uncertainty-quantification methods gave radiative-heating uncertainties between 30% and 100% (Hansson, RHTGSM workshop, 24 Sep 2026). For Earth return at ~12 km/s, heating exceeds 3,000 W/cm2 and radiation becomes a first-order load (ESA).
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: AI can build state-resolved excitation and dissociation kinetics from ab initio potential surfaces and shock-tube data, then reduce them to engineering models with error bounds. This is partly open physics (heavy-particle excitation was the missing term at SRL) and partly expensive expert work. Family 275 (QMA-hardness of continuum Coulomb energies, T1) is a ceiling: no general exact first-principles shortcut exists. EAST shot rate is the physical gate.

bottlenecks.name: Material response: ablation, pyrolysis, gas-surface interaction, char failure, reusable tile durability
bottlenecks.description: Material-property uncertainty dominates TPS thickness. In NASA's SRL design, PICA-D conductivity carries a 2-sigma uncertainty of about 32% and the material margin dominates the RSS thickness (Alpert et al., IPPW 2026). Failure modes escape the models. Artemis I's Avcoat char loss came from insufficient permeability, and finding it took 121 tests across 8 campaigns (NASA). Recession models such as PATO match plasma-tunnel data to about +/-20% (ESA conference, 2026). For reusable tiles (Starship, ~18,000 tiles), the problem is cracking, edge damage, hot-gas ingress at tile boundaries and bond fatigue across flights (Flight 13 reporting, Jul-Aug 2026).
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Homogenization from pore scale to volume average, inverse calibration of properties from arc-jet data, and failure criteria are partly open and largely expert-scarce. Inverse-problem theory for inspection gets a direct boost from catalog families 365 (T3), 372 (T1) and 366 (T1). The physical gate is arc-jet hours: the Ames Arc Jet Complex is NASA's only ground facility for reentry TPS testing. Reflight count gates reusable-tile models.

bottlenecks.name: Margins, uncertainty quantification and ground-to-flight extrapolation
bottlenecks.description: Designers stack deterministic factors. For SRL: a convective heat-flux factor of 1.22 forebody and 2.0 aftbody, radiative 1.5 and 1.47, a 20% recession margin, and a bondline margin. NASA's own alternative-margining study shows that a heat shield at ~75% of baseline thickness still gives 99% confidence that the bondline stays below its allowable (Alpert et al., IPPW 2026). Model-form error in extrapolating from arc-jet to flight is the genuinely hard part.
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Mostly solved in principle but expert-scarce: joint probabilistic margins, reliability-based sizing, Bayesian optimal experimental design and model-form error bounds. This is the fastest AI unlock in the domain (P1, then P5). It is gated by adoption: program margin policy and the risk culture after Artemis I.

bottlenecks.name: EDL guidance and powered descent: supersonic retropropulsion, aerocapture guidance, precision landing
bottlenecks.description: All of NASA's 20 t human-scale Mars lander concepts rely on supersonic retropropulsion (NASA EDL Architecture Study). The interaction between plume and freestream is unsteady and hard to test at scale on Earth. Aerocapture has never flown: NASA is studying an Earth demonstration, including a $350k Inversion study through June 2027 (Sep 2026), and Uranus studies find MSL-heritage aeroshells adequate but require a risk-reduction flight demo first.
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Guidance with proofs (convex powered-descent guidance, robust predictor-corrector aerocapture guidance) is formal-verification work: P2, gated by qualification. Aero-propulsive SRP models are applied-math work gated by data, since full-scale flight data comes only from Falcon 9 and Starship and is proprietary.

bottlenecks.name: Rarefied, kinetic and plasma effects: DSMC versus Boltzmann, high-altitude aerocapture passes, RF blackout
bottlenecks.description: DSMC codes (SPARTA and others) are the workhorse for transitional flow, with Fokker-Planck variants now cheaper. Rarefied heating matters most for aerocapture and early entry. Blackout is a coupled problem of nonequilibrium ionization and electromagnetics. Starship relays telemetry through Starlink, and magnetic windows remain at the screening-model stage (Lieu, arXiv 2608.10018, Aug 2026).
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Families 363 (nonuniqueness) and 364 (kinetic limit with fluctuations) are manuscript-only (T1). If they hold, they change confidence in kinetic models and mark where a selection principle is needed. They change no numbers. Error-controlled hybrid kinetic solvers and coupled EM-plasma link analysis are expert-scarce engineering math that AI could make routine.

hyper.scenario_contrast: Working assumption for the shared nodes (owned elsewhere): cap-research-math-public arrives in 2028 in S1 and 2027 in S2/S3; cap-applied-math in 2029/2027/2027; cap-physics-theory after 2031 in S1, 2029 in S2, 2028 in S3; cap-design-optimization 2031/2029/2028; cap-autonomous-labs after 2031, 2029, 2028; infra-mathlib-applied 2030/2028/2027; infra-verified-numerics after 2031, 2029, 2028; infra-tool-qualification after 2031, 2030, 2029. Moving from S1 to S2 shifts the domain's tier-2 nodes (stability analysis, test design, margin UQ, inverse NDE) 1-2 years earlier and up one band, because they are solved in principle but expert-scarce and only the cognitive clock binds. Tier-3 physics nodes (transition, SBLI closures, radiation kinetics, gas-surface chemistry, ablator response) move about 2 years in S2. They stay at Low or Medium because each needs physical calibration: arc-jet hours at what is NASA's only reentry TPS facility, EAST shock-tube shots, and a few transition flights a year. The flight-data node grows linearly, not exponentially, in every scenario. Tier 5-7 nodes barely move: rapid reuse and Mars landing are paced by flight count, synodic windows and SpaceX strategy, and point-to-point by regulation. The commercial-capsule chain (UQ, then probabilistic sizing, then a thinner flown TPS) is the one place where S2 turns into flown hardware before 2031, because capsules iterate every few months and need no certification body to accept margins. S3 adds autonomous experiments and AI-accelerated programs from ~2028, which helps materials and chemistry calibration and gives a small lift to whole-program outcomes such as the Mars landing (Low to Medium). It cannot create arc jets, launch windows or range approvals.
key_insights: The biggest near-term lever in entry systems is margins, not a theorem. NASA's own SRL study (IPPW 2026) shows a heat shield at ~75% of baseline thickness still meets 99% bondline-temperature confidence. Rigorous joint UQ is solved in principle but expert-scarce, the classic case where on-demand AI mathematics pays first (P1, then P5).

The domain is bound by validation data, not cognition. The arc jet (NASA's only reentry TPS facility), the EAST shock tube and a few transition flights a year set the slope. AI's highest-value early role is test design that maximizes information per run, multiplying the physical gate instead of pretending to bypass it.

Radiative heating is the largest physics gap for fast entries. At SRL's 8 km/s, baseline models under-predicted VUV by up to 2x against EAST, and UQ methods disagreed between 30% and 100% (Sep 2026). AI-built kinetics can plausibly halve that by 2030 in S2, but family 275 (T1) caps first-principles shortcuts and shock-tube time binds.

The openai/math catalog contributes little directly. Families 363 and 364 (T1) change confidence in DSMC and Boltzmann modeling; 365 (T3), 372 and 366 (T1) inform heat-shield inspection theory, with 365's conductivity nonuniqueness the most actionable as a P3 design rule (do not rely on thermal boundary data alone); 275 and 278 (T1) are ceilings on ab initio chemistry. None changes a heating number.

Starship rapid reuse and the first heavy Mars landing are paced by hardware and launch windows. AI mathematics shifts them by months at most, and only two Mars launch opportunities remain before end-2031 (about late 2028 and early 2031).

The fastest chain from AI mathematics to flown hardware runs through commercial capsules (Varda-class, flying every few months with instrumented heat shields): AI-run UQ, then probabilistic sizing, then thinner flown TPS, plausibly by 2029 in S2.
Formal verification reaches EDL through guidance software and numerics kernels, not aerothermal physics, and is capped by tool qualification (around 2030-31 even in S2).

In S2 the main structural change is that analysis stops being scarce. A small company can carry the analysis load of a NASA center (aerocapture demo, new capsules, deployables), but capital and launch access then become the gates.
nil_effects: Entry energy budget: ~30 MJ/kg from LEO, ~72 MJ/kg at 12 km/s. Physics fixes how much energy must be dissipated, so TPS cannot be designed away, only right-sized.

Ground-test capacity: no scenario builds new arc jets or shock tubes fast. The Ames Arc Jet Complex is NASA's only reentry TPS ground facility, and DoD calls hypersonic test capacity a national bottleneck. AI can only use the hours better.
Mars synodic windows: only two launch opportunities before end-2031. Cognition does not add windows.

Material capability: better theory does not make PICA, Avcoat or ceramic tiles better. New TPS materials need fabrication, arc-jet and flight qualification on a 5-10 year clock, though autonomous labs in S3 compress discovery but not qualification.
Galactic speedups: family 107 (matrix-multiplication exponent 9/4 or below) and family 130 (FFT below n log n) give no practical speedup to CFD, DSMC or radiation solvers.
Family 362 (relativistic Vlasov-Maxwell smoothness, T3) has no bearing on reentry plasma sheaths or blackout. The sheath is collisional, weakly ionized and non-relativistic.

Family 376 and the separate Sep 2026 forced Navier-Stokes blowup claim: forced-flow results say nothing about hypersonic heating, transition or turbulence closures, which remain closure-and-data problems.
Well-posedness results (363, 364, 362) change confidence in models, not predicted heat fluxes or TPS thickness.
Regulatory and range gates for point-to-point transport (overflight, sonic boom, landing-site environmental reviews, host-nation rights) and FAA reentry licensing are untouched.
Classified defense hypersonic flight data will not flow to civil model builders because of better mathematics, so civil model calibration stays data-poor.

signposts.event: Outside teams can buy research-grade math capability (OpenAI or another lab) by mid-2027
signposts.what_it_changes: Confirms S2 timing for all P1 nodes (stability analysis, test design, margin UQ, inverse NDE). If public access slips past 2028, shift these nodes one year later and down one band, toward S1.

signposts.event: Expert review or a Comparator check of families 363/364 (Boltzmann) and 365 (inverse problems) within 12 months
signposts.what_it_changes: Moves hyper-boltzmann-foundations-check to T2/T4 and settles whether the nonuniqueness is entropy-admissible. A refutation removes the kinetic catalog links but leaves the capability-driven nodes unchanged.

signposts.event: A NASA, ESA or commercial program adopts reliability-based TPS sizing (margin-policy revision, design-review citation, or a capsule operator disclosure)
signposts.what_it_changes: Confirms the margins chain (hyper-probabilistic-tps-sizing to hyper-thinner-tps-flown) and supports pulling the S2 flown date to 2028-29.

signposts.event: First Starship ship catch and reflight, with published heat-shield turnaround and tile-replacement counts (2027?)
signposts.what_it_changes: Sets the real data clock for hyper-tile-damage-accumulation and hyper-rapid-reuse-heatshield. A new TPS architecture announcement would push both out by years.

signposts.event: A blind or flight-validated AI-assisted transition prediction (BOLT-1B follow-ons, MACH-TB flights)
signposts.what_it_changes: Raises hyper-transition-prediction-theory from Low toward Medium in S2. Failure confirms the data gate dominates.

signposts.event: AI-generated radiation kinetics match EAST VUV spectra within 20% without tuning, at a radiation workshop or IPPW
signposts.what_it_changes: Raises hyper-radiation-kinetics and the 12+ km/s design basis. It would justify lowering radiative heating factors from ~1.5 toward ~1.25.

signposts.event: NASA awards an aerocapture flight demonstration after the Inversion study ends (June 2027)
signposts.what_it_changes: Makes hyper-aerocapture-demo Medium or better in S1. Without an award by 2028, all aerocapture outcome nodes stay Low or Speculative.

signposts.event: Mathlib or another proof library gains substantial PDE and numerical-analysis coverage (Sobolev spaces, finite-volume convergence, floating-point semantics) during 2027
signposts.what_it_changes: Pulls hyper-verified-aerothermal-numerics and hyper-certified-edl-guidance earlier. Slow coverage keeps them after 2031 in S1.

signposts.event: SpaceX commits a Starship to the late-2028 Mars window and demonstrates ship-to-ship propellant transfer
signposts.what_it_changes: Moves hyper-mars-heavy-landing from 2031 to 2029 in all scenarios. That would be a physical-clock change, not an AI-mathematics one.

bottlenecks.name: Qualification and design allowables (physical evidence burden)
bottlenecks.description: Turning a promising material or process into flight-qualified hardware: multi-heat/multi-lot coupon programs for A/B-basis allowables, per-machine qualification under NASA-STD-6030 ('a new process means a new material'), witness testing, CT inspection, handbook (MMPDS, CMH-17) and customer acceptance. Historical insertion takes 10-20+ years (>20 years and ~$400M for aerospace per MGI-era estimates; GE ~2 decades and >$1B for CMCs; GRCop 1987 to 2023 flight).
bottlenecks.share_of_effort: ~30% of materials-program time and cost (analyst estimate, general)
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Medium. The statistics (hierarchical Bayesian tolerance bounds, transfer across machines and lots) are solved in principle but expert-scarce, so on-demand AI helps quickly; but physical lots and regulator acceptance bind, so calendar savings need the evidence rules to change.

bottlenecks.name: Process-structure-property modeling for printed metals and composites
bottlenecks.description: Predicting porosity, microstructure, residual stress and fatigue/creep scatter from process parameters and sensor data across scales (melt pool to part), for AM alloys (GRCop-42, GRX-810, NASA HR-1), CMCs and ablators.
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Medium-high. Mix of genuinely open math (quantitative homogenization for nonlinear random media, extreme-value defect statistics) and expert-scarce applied work (inverse calibration, UQ). Paired sensor/CT/fatigue data bind once the math is cheap.

bottlenecks.name: Long-duration degradation and life prediction
bottlenecks.description: Creep, oxidation and thermomechanical fatigue of hot-section alloys and TPS; perovskite and III-V PV degradation; battery capacity fade under ~5,500 LEO cycles a year. Real-time tests (a 10,000-hour creep test is ~14 months; a year in orbit is a year) are the physical clock.
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Medium. AI can build mechanism-based kinetic models and quantify acceleration factors, but cannot compress the real-time exposure needed to validate them.

bottlenecks.name: Radiation effects in electronics (single-event effects and dose)
bottlenecks.description: Predicting and mitigating single-event upsets, latch-up, burnout and total-dose effects for rad-hard parts and, increasingly, commercial accelerators (GPUs/TPUs/HBM) for orbital compute; beam-test campaigns at a few facilities; SiC/GaN power-device derating.
bottlenecks.share_of_effort: ~12% overall; much higher for COTS-heavy orbital-compute programs (analyst estimate, general)
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Medium-high. Hierarchical stochastic error models and formal verification of fault-tolerance layers are bespoke applied math and P2 work that AI does well; beam time and on-orbit statistics bind.

bottlenecks.name: Electronic-structure fidelity and cost (the DFT layer)
bottlenecks.description: Uncontrolled exchange-correlation errors (~3-5 kcal/mol for hybrids), strongly correlated systems (transition-metal oxides, defects), finite-temperature thermodynamics and the cost of high-level reference data; the foundation under alloy, ceramic, PV, battery and propellant screening.
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Low directly (the catalog's 278/275/263 are ceilings, P3), high indirectly: learned functionals, certified MLIP uncertainty and quantum-algorithm resource reduction are where AI math and AI models combine.

bottlenecks.name: Synthesis and characterization throughput
bottlenecks.description: Making and correctly identifying candidate materials: autonomous labs (Periodic Labs, Lila, DeepMind UK, A-Lab), synthesizability prediction, and reliable structure refinement (the A-Lab/GNoME critiques showed automated Rietveld and disorder handling are weak links).
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Medium. Inverse-problem identifiability, Bayesian refinement and experimental design are AI-suited; robots, furnaces and neutron/synchrotron access bind.

materials.scenario_contrast: S1 (plateau): AI math stays mostly in proofs; research-grade applied math reaches outside teams ~2029. The front of the tree (tiers 1-4) is mostly Medium or Low by 2031, AI-designed flight hardware is Low or Speculative, and tiers 6-7 are Speculative; progress continues through existing machine learning (MLIPs, ICME) without the new math layer. S2 (exponential, base case): the cognitive clock compresses hard. Certified MLIP uncertainty, reliable automated characterization and system-level radiation-error models arrive 2027-28; learned functionals and AI alloy, TPS and propellant design by 2028; nearly all tier 2-4 nodes reach High or Medium by 2031. Then physical gates bind on every tier-5+ node: one year in orbit for PV, hot-fire and creep hours for alloys, hazard and compatibility tests for propellants, beam time for electronics, handbook committees for allowables. Result: first AI-designed alloy and TPS flights ~2029-30 (Medium), rad-tolerant commercial orbital compute operating with model-sized mitigation from 2028 (High), and fleet-level outcomes (insertion under five years, a power-per-kilogram step) after 2031. S3 (recursive): adds near-free cognition and autonomous labs at scale from 2028. It moves tier 2-4 nodes ~0-1 year earlier than S2 and pulls a few downstream nodes (alloy flight, SiC power devices, propellant flight, quantum chemistry) forward by about a year, but cannot compress orbital exposure, creep hours, beam time or regulatory cycles, so tier 6-7 bands barely move (only quantum chemistry and insertion-time compression gain a band). The S1-to-S2 gap is large (~1-2 years and about one band on tiers 2-5); the S2-to-S3 gap is small (about a year on a handful of nodes).
key_insights: The catalog barely touches this domain directly. Its three electronic-structure results (278 Kohn-Sham ensemble non-representability, 275 QMA-hardness of continuum Coulomb energy, 263 ionization bounds) are ceilings that formalize what practitioners already believed: DFT is uncontrolled and no efficient universal method exists. They act fast (P3) but change no code or flown material; their practical message is to invest in domain-specific, data-driven methods.

The capability is what matters (analyst position a): most of the math this domain needs is bespoke and expert-scarce (uncertainty for ML interatomic models, Bayesian allowables, radiation-error models, degradation kinetics), not a famous conjecture. The genuinely open problems are few and specific: quantitative homogenization for nonlinear random microstructures, and the mechanism of single-event burnout in SiC.

Cognition is a small share of materials insertion time. Ferrium M54 was designed in under a year but took under six years to flight qualification; GRCop went from 1987 to a 2023 flight; AF-M315E took more than 20 years. Even free cognition shortens insertion only ~20-30% unless the evidence rules themselves change, so the highest-value AI-math unlocks here are statistical and verification frameworks that let regulators accept fewer physical tests.

Under the exponential base case (S2), the cognitive clock compresses hard: nearly all tier 2-4 nodes reach High or Medium by 2031. But every tier-5+ node is bound by a physical clock (a year in orbit for PV, hot-fire and creep hours for alloys, hazard and compatibility testing for propellants, beam time for electronics, handbook committees for allowables). First AI-designed alloy and TPS flights land ~2029-30 at Medium; fleet-level outcomes land after 2031.

S3 adds little beyond S2 in this domain: across 30 nodes the 2031 band count moves from 11 High / 12 Medium / 6 Low / 1 Speculative (S2) to 11 / 14 / 4 / 1 (S3), versus 0 / 11 / 10 / 9 in S1. The S1-to-S2 gap (~1-2 years and about one band on tiers 2-5) dwarfs the S2-to-S3 gap, the clearest sign that physics and institutions, not cognition, bind.

The fastest space payoff is in electronics, not materials: rad-tolerant commercial AI chips for orbital compute face commercial (not regulatory) gates and short test cycles, and the math involved (system-level error models, verified fault tolerance) is exactly what AI does well. Knowing true error rates can let operators swap triple redundancy (~3x overhead) for algorithm-based fault tolerance (~5-20%), roughly 2.5x more useful compute per watt (general).

Discovery is not space's bottleneck; qualification is. Autonomous labs (Periodic Labs, Lila, DeepMind UK) will flood the front of the pipeline, and the A-Lab/GNoME critiques show characterization is the hidden weak link. Without qualification compression, more candidates only lengthen the queue.

Risk-tolerant commercial actors fly AI-designed materials first (self-certifying engine makers, capsule operators like Varda flying a reentry every few months, orbital-compute startups); NASA Class A and crewed systems trail by 3-5+ years because certification caps their bands at Medium.

Quantum computing for chemistry stays outside the 2031 window except in S3: Quantinuum-SoftBank (Jul 2026) put chemically accurate >100-spin-orbital simulation in the 2030s, and 275 and 265 cut against universal quantum advantage. AI math's lever is algorithmic resource reduction, which could pull one beyond-classical result to ~2029-30 under S3.
nil_effects: Real-time physical clocks do not compress: 10,000-hour creep tests, a year of on-orbit PV exposure, ~5,500 LEO battery cycles a year, beam time at a handful of facilities. Under S2/S3 these become the critical path for every tier-5+ node.

Thermodynamic and detailed-balance limits are untouched: no theorem raises the efficiency ceiling of III-V or perovskite cells (commercial III-V >29.5% AM0, record ~34% triple junction) or the thermochemical ceiling on chemical-propellant specific impulse; AI-designed propellants gain mainly in handling, toxicity and density (single-digit percent).
Deployed DFT codes and materials workflows will not change because of 278, 275 or 263; ceiling theorems change method-development priorities, not practice.

The radiation environment does not change: galactic cosmic-ray heavy ions still cause single-event effects in scaled CMOS, and shielding against them remains mass-limited; math can only right-size mitigation.
Galactic algorithms in the release (107 matrix multiplication, 130 FFT) give no speedup to materials simulation, MLIP training or onboard compute.

Qualification regimes (NASA-STD-6030, MMPDS, CMH-17, ECSS) change on committee cycles of years; even S3 cannot make a handbook committee meet faster, which caps every certification-dependent node at Medium.

Supply chains and fabs are untouched: powder atomization lots, the few rad-hard and wide-bandgap fabs, germanium substrates for III-V cells, and energetics-licensed labs set lead times that AI cognition does not shorten.

No theorem says an ambient-pressure superconductor with Tc above 77 K exists; autonomous labs (Periodic Labs' north star) may search faster, but physics may forbid one, so it stays a speculative wildcard outside this tree.
Quantum chemistry advantage is not a 2031 story in S1/S2: 275 (QMA-hardness) rules out universal speedups, and fault-tolerant hardware is a fabrication gate.

physclock.domain: Calibrating the physical clock: how fast atoms, tests and institutions can move

bottlenecks.name: Test, qualification and certification campaigns
bottlenecks.description: Environmental qualification (vibration, acoustic, shock, thermal vacuum, EMI), engine hot-fire campaigns, materials allowables, human rating and reliability demonstration. Evidence is generated in physical time and counted under standards (NASA-STD-7009, GEVS, SMC-S-016, ECSS-E-ST-10-03, NASA-STD-6030) that do not yet say what AI-made analysis is worth.
bottlenecks.share_of_effort: ~25-35% of a new system's critical path (integration and test ~25% plus qualification and reviews ~10%, illustrative, general); larger for crewed, nuclear and new-material programs
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Mixed. Solved in principle but expert-scarce: information-optimal test design, test-data reduction, model correlation, anomaly diagnosis; on-demand AI is the unlock (2027-28 in S2). Genuinely open: credible uncertainty quantification for rare events and model-form error, certified multiphysics numerics, and the institutional rule for counting analysis as evidence (NASA's own aircraft certification-by-analysis roadmap targets 2040-2050). No catalog family moves this directly.

bottlenecks.name: Fabrication, production ramp and supply chain
bottlenecks.description: Building engines, stages, satellites and test articles; ramping lines to rate; long-lead radiation-hardened parts, forgings, castings, solid motors and nuclear fuel; factory and tooling capex.
bottlenecks.share_of_effort: ~20-30% of a typical critical path (fabrication and procurement ~25%, general); the binding gate on cadence for constellations and reusable fleets (Mach33 found New Glenn cadence gated by BE-4 and upper-stage production, not reuse)
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Small. Generative design for manufacturability and additive-manufacturing process models help at the margin; AI-run factories and robotics matter only in S3. Rad-hard parts (12-24+ months), single-source suppliers, HALEU fuel and capex are physical.

bottlenecks.name: Flight-test iteration and reuse learning
bottlenecks.description: Hardware-rich build-fly-fix loops for new vehicles, mishap investigations, and the accumulation of flight cycles needed to extend reuse life and prove reliability.
bottlenecks.share_of_effort: For new launch vehicles, roughly 40-60% of post-design schedule (Starship: 14 integrated flights in 41 months, 48-90 day loops in 2025, 63-66 days in 2026); for reuse economics, the gate that sets $/kg
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Moderate on the cognitive slice only: anomaly diagnosis and probabilistic life models (days instead of weeks). Zero on flight count: Falcon 9 needed 15 months from first landing to first reflight, and cohort lifetimes rose from 4.2 flights (2018 boosters) to 24 (2020 boosters) one flight at a time.

bottlenecks.name: Launch access, cadence and cost per kilogram
bottlenecks.description: Manifest slots, pad and range capacity, propellant logistics, and the price of mass to orbit, which together gate every mass-heavy downstream application.
bottlenecks.share_of_effort: ~5-10% of schedule for most spacecraft (waiting for a slot), but the dominant economic gate for mass-heavy missions; Amazon Leo had reached about 11% of its FCC deployment milestone by Jan 2026
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Indirect only. Mach33 attributes the fall from $4,915/kg (expended Flight 14) to $656/kg (2027 base) 56% to reuse, 32% to payload and 12% to production learning. None is a mathematics problem; AI helps through faster anomaly closure and life models.

bottlenecks.name: Regulation and licensing
bottlenecks.description: FAA Part 450 launch and reentry licenses, NEPA environmental reviews for new sites and higher cadence, FCC and ITU spectrum, presidential-level approval for nuclear launches (NSPM-20), export control and human-rating reviews.
bottlenecks.share_of_effort: ~5-15% of schedule overall; on the critical path for new vehicles, new sites and nuclear systems (environmental assessment 1-2 years, EIS 2-4 years, 180-day statutory license review after a complete application, general)
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: High for preparation: flight-safety analyses and environmental documents are expert-scarce, solved-in-principle work. Real for regulator-side review capacity. Zero for statutory clocks, public comment, litigation and politics. Reform is already under way without AI (EO 14335, Aug 2025; FAA proposed rules Jul 30 and Oct 5 2026; FCC Part 100, Jul 2026).

bottlenecks.name: Capital and program funding
bottlenecks.description: Appropriations cycles and political decisions for government programs; equity and debt for commercial programs.
bottlenecks.share_of_effort: Sets the pace of government programs (Artemis II slipped 5-7 years; Mars Sample Return, Gateway and DRACO cancelled 2025-26) and of every non-SpaceX commercial program; not binding for SpaceX ($100.8B cash after its June 2026 IPO)
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Cuts the engineering-labor share of development cost by roughly 15-30% under S2; does not change appropriations, politics or the hardware and facility share of cost.

physclock.scenario_contrast: Two clocks, and two exponentials. The physical exponential in space is already running and owes nothing to AI math: Starship reached orbit on Sep 28 2026, first reflights are expected in early 2027, and Mach33's base case takes SpaceX's internal cost from ~$4,915/kg (expended Flight 14) to ~$656/kg in 2027, ~$300/kg in 2028 and $13/kg by 2035, driven by reuse, payload and production learning. That curve, internal cost under $300/kg (2028) and pads and propellant plants for hundreds of flights (2028), is the same in S1, S2 and S3. S1 (Plateau): AI is a consulting-grade analyst from 2028; physical gates compress 0-5%; 100+ heavy flights a year arrive around 2030; institutional relaxers (credibility standards, analysis credit, reuse acceptance for crew and national-security missions) stay beyond 2031; programs run 10-20% shorter. S2 (Exponential, base case): cognitive work runs 5-10x faster from 2028, which collapses the cognitive slices that sit on the physical critical path: anomaly diagnosis (days instead of weeks), license analyses and agency review (weeks instead of months), test-campaign design (20-40% fewer tests). Experiment and fabrication gates compress only 1.1-1.3x, so tier 5-6 nodes move by 0-1 year, and institutional nodes move 1-2+ years earlier (credibility standard 2029, analysis credit and qualification compression 2030) but stay capped at Medium. Programs started in 2028 or later are ~30-40% shorter, consistent with capability-program-cycle-compression. S3 (Recursive): cognitive work is close to free from about 2029, and AI-run test stands and factories lift the physical multiplier to ~1.3-1.5x; heavy cadence reaches 100+ in 2028 and the customer price under $1,000/kg arrives about 2030, but flight cycles for reuse life, real-time endurance tests, statutory clocks, appropriations and orbital mechanics stay fixed. Across scenarios the ordering of the tree barely changes; what changes is how much of the remaining schedule is pure physics. Under S2 by 2029, more than ~80% of the critical path of a hardware-rich program is physical time.
key_insights: The launch-cost exponential is real, already under way, and independent of AI math. Mach33 attributes the 2026-27 Starship cost decline 56% to reuse, 32% to payload and 12% to production learning; AI moves internal cost by at most 0-1 year in any scenario. The client's 'exponential curve' for space through 2031 is mainly this physical one, and AI math rides on it rather than driving it.

Amdahl's law sets the ceiling. With roughly a third of a program's critical path cognitive and physical gates compressing 1.1-1.3x in S2, new programs run ~30-40% shorter, not 10x. The cognitive slices that matter most sit inside physical loops: mishap diagnosis, license analysis, test design and data reduction.

Announced schedules run long by 1.5-3x, and the slips are physical. Flight 12 took ~2.8 times Musk's 'six weeks'; New Glenn flew five years after its 2020 target; Neutron slipped from NET Jul 2025 to NET Q4 2026; Artemis II flew 5-7 years after its original window. The causes were hardware failures, pad damage and funding, which AI does not remove.

The highest-leverage relaxer of the physical clock is institutional, not physical: a rule for what AI-made analysis is worth (credibility standards, then certification by analysis). In S2 it lands around 2029-30, capped at Medium, while NASA's own aviation roadmap says 2040-2050. Every 'replace tests with analysis' node in other domains should sit downstream of physclock-credibility-evidence-standard.

Regulation is moving without AI: EO 14335 (Aug 2025), FAA proposed rules (Jul 30 and Oct 5 2026), the FCC's Part 100 (Jul 2026), and a draft assessment raising New Glenn's cap from 12 to 50 launches a year. AI adds preparation speed and reviewer capacity; statutory clocks (180 days), public comment and litigation stay fixed.

Reuse learning is bought one flight at a time. Falcon 9 cohort lifetimes went from 4.2 flights (2018) to 24 (2020); Mach33's Starship base goes from 3.3 flights per stack (2027) to 18 (2030). Data-driven reflight clearance can pull this forward 6-12 months (worth ~$1-2B on the 2028 Starlink manifest) but cannot replace flight cycles.

Capital is not binding for the leader and is binding for everyone else. SpaceX held $100.8B in cash after its $85.7B June 2026 IPO and has spent over $15B on Starship; new entrants raise in $0.1-1B rounds. A 15-30% AI cut in development labor cost matters far more to entrants than to SpaceX, but the customer price per kilogram still follows competitor cadence (Mach33: a one-year cadence delay moves external crossover about a year).

Lag ladder for other domains (S2): from design-complete to first flight, a smallsat or derivative payload takes 12-18 months, a new launch-vehicle subsystem 2-3 years, a new engine 4-6 years, a crewed system 5+ years, a space reactor 4-6 years from a funded start. No tier-5 or tier-6 node whose design depends on 2027-28 AI capability should fly before about 2029 (smallsat) or 2031+ (new engine or primary structure).

Government flagships remain politically clocked: Mars Sample Return ($7B and 2033, then $11B and 2040, then cancelled 2026), Gateway (cancelled Mar 2026), DRACO (cancelled 2025, with cheaper launch cited) and SR-1 Freedom ($2.1B estimate, $10M directed). No scenario compresses appropriations.

Method note: the session's WebSearch budget was exhausted and the Firecrawl account was out of credits, so this research used direct page fetches (Wikipedia, NTRS, Federal Register, White House, NASA, MGI) and the 33FG/Mach33 research MCP; items marked (general) are unsourced background knowledge.
nil_effects: Launch cost per kilogram through 2031 follows reuse rate, payload and production learning; AI math moves it by 0-1 year at most.
Propellant logistics and cost: about 389 cryogen truck deliveries per Starship flight on merchant supply, and air-separation plants, pipelines and power, all built on the physical clock (Mach33).
Real-time endurance testing: creep (a 10,000-hour test is ~14 months), thermal-vacuum cycling, electric-thruster life tests of thousands of hours, and radiation dose tests at accelerator flux limits.

Reliability demonstration by test: with zero failures, showing 0.99 reliability at 90% confidence needs about 230 successful trials (n = ln(0.1)/ln(0.99)); only accepted model-based priors change this, which is a regulatory, not a mathematical, step.
Orbital mechanics: Mars departure windows every ~26 months (late 2026, early 2029, 2031) and 6-9 month transits; no compute shortens them.
Statutory and procedural clocks: the 180-day Part 450 review, NEPA comment periods and species consultations, ITU coordination milestones, and presidential nuclear launch approval.
Government appropriations and political decisions (Gateway, Mars Sample Return and DRACO cancellations; SR-1's $10M against a $2.1B estimate).
Pad, test-stand and large test-facility construction (2-4 years each) and scarce facilities such as arc jets and large thermal-vacuum chambers.
Human-rating risk posture: crewed flight tests and independent review boards are not shortened by better analysis.
Long-lead physical supply: radiation-hardened parts (12-24+ months), forgings and castings, solid rocket motors and HALEU nuclear fuel.
Failure statistics: a pad-destroying failure (New Glenn, May 28 2026) costs about a year regardless of how fast the root cause is found.

signposts.event: Flight 15 ship catch (about Dec 2026) and first reflight of a caught Starship booster and ship by mid-2027
signposts.what_it_changes: Confirms physclock-starship-full-reuse and the Mach33 base cost path ($656/kg 2027, ~$300/kg 2028); a failed catch with no ship reflight before mid-2027 moves the tree to the bear path and pushes cadence and cost nodes a year later.

signposts.event: Starship flight count in 2027 (12 or more) and LC-39A's first Starship launch
signposts.what_it_changes: Confirms physclock-flight-test-cadence and the 2028 pad milestone; fewer than eight flights pushes heavy-cadence-100 to 2030-31 in every scenario.

signposts.event: About 1,000 Starlink V3 satellites in orbit by Q2 2027 (Musk to investors, Aug 2026)
signposts.what_it_changes: Requires roughly 17-40 Starship flights by mid-2027; meeting it would pull heavy-cadence-100 forward a year, missing it confirms the physical clock binds.

signposts.event: FAA final rules on the Jul 30 and Oct 5 2026 Part 450 proposals, and the final New Glenn 12-to-50 assessment
signposts.what_it_changes: Confirms physclock-licensing-in-weeks is reform-driven; published evaluation times under 120 days would move it to High.

signposts.event: A NASA-STD-7009 revision, NASA engineering directive or ECSS note on AI-generated analysis evidence; a CM4QC pilot granting qualification credit
signposts.what_it_changes: Pulls physclock-credibility-evidence-standard to 2028 and the analysis-credit and qualification-compression nodes up a year; absence through 2028 confirms the S1 timing even if the cognitive clock follows S2.

signposts.event: An operator publicly crediting AI with a mishap root cause, followed by return to flight within weeks
signposts.what_it_changes: Confirms physclock-ai-mishap-analysis in S2 timing.

signposts.event: New Glenn return to flight after the pad rebuild, Neutron's first launch, and Chinese reusable cadence in 2027
signposts.what_it_changes: Sets physclock-reusable-competition and therefore the customer-price node; another year of slips pushes customer prices under $1,000/kg beyond 2031 in S2.

signposts.event: FY2027 appropriation for SR-1 Freedom of several hundred million dollars, and HALEU fuel deliveries
signposts.what_it_changes: Moves physclock-reactor-in-space toward 2029 (Medium); a token appropriation moves it beyond 2031 in all scenarios.

signposts.event: Published Starship third-party pricing or more contracts like Voyager's (~$900/kg)
signposts.what_it_changes: Tests whether the customer price fades on Mach33's 2033 midpoint or earlier.

signposts.event: A propulsion or test-services firm reporting autonomous around-the-clock test operations with utilization above 70%
signposts.what_it_changes: Confirms physclock-ai-run-test-stands and the physical multiplier assumed for S2 and S3.

plasma.domain: Plasma: electric propulsion, fusion propulsion and space weather

bottlenecks.name: Electron-transport closure in Hall thrusters and other EP devices
bottlenecks.description: Every engineering Hall-thruster code needs an empirical 'anomalous' electron collision frequency calibrated to each operating point. A single calibrated model predicts SPT-140 thrust within ~7% and discharge current within ~15% (8% and 17% when extrapolated to orbit), and whole-device kinetic simulation that could resolve the physics is not affordable (Whittaker et al., AIAA 2026). The same closure gap governs magnetic nozzles (VASIMR, helicon, fusion-drive exhausts).
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Mixed. The closure itself is a genuinely open physics problem (about 60 years old). AI's route to it runs through affordable kinetic simulation (algorithm invention: expert-scarce rather than open) plus theory that reduces the simulations to a closure. Bayesian calibration, UQ and implicit-PIC design are solved in principle but expert-scarce and become on-demand in 2027-28 under S2. Validation needs non-invasive electron diagnostics and low-pressure facility time, which bind.

bottlenecks.name: Ground-to-flight extrapolation and life qualification
bottlenecks.description: Thrusters are tested in chambers whose background gas shifts performance (SPT-140 thrust ~2-4% higher at 10 microtorr than at the lowest pressure; Mackey et al. 2018) and must prove life by wear tests. AEPS must demonstrate 1,770 kg of xenon throughput plus 50% margin and is still preparing its long-duration life test, a decade after contract award; crewed-Mars-class MPD thrusters need >23,000 h (2.6 years) of operation. Wear tests are the longest pole in EP schedules.
bottlenecks.share_of_effort: ~20% of modeling effort, and most of the schedule and cost of a new thruster program (judgment)
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Mostly expert-scarce rather than open: erosion prediction needs near-wall plasma properties (which depend on the transport closure) and low-energy sputter-yield data (a materials-experiment problem). AI helps build credible predictive wear models with UQ; the binding gates are test hours and whether NASA/ESA accept model-based life credit.

bottlenecks.name: Solar eruption and CME propagation forecasting
bottlenecks.description: CME arrival-time error has stayed near 13 h mean absolute error for 11 years (Kay et al. 2024); the storm-driving southward field Bz is known only when the CME passes L1, roughly 30-60 minutes before impact; flare forecasting beyond a few hours is still largely statistical. Kay et al. attribute errors to input reconstruction (few viewpoints, no routine coronal magnetic-field measurement) and to the background solar wind.
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Partly open physics (eruption onset, flux-rope evolution), partly expert-scarce applied math (ensemble data assimilation, regularized inverse problems for the coronal field). The dominant limit is observational: new viewpoints (ESA Vigil at L5, launch planned 2031) matter more than mathematics.

bottlenecks.name: Upper-atmosphere density and drag prediction
bottlenecks.description: Density is the largest LEO orbit-prediction error: empirical models disagree by 20-40% in quiet times and storms raise density 2-6x within hours (Gannon storm, May 2024: decay of tracked objects 38 -> 180 m/day, Ap forecasts underpredicted by 100-300, thousands of satellites maneuvering). In Feb 2022 a G2 storm cost 38 of 49 newly launched Starlink satellites at ~210 km. Density drives conjunction assessment, constellation propellant budgets and VLEO viability.
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Largely solved in principle but expert-scarce: joint estimation of density and unknown ballistic coefficients from thousands of constellation orbits, model-error estimation, and propagation of uncertainty into covariance. This is where on-demand applied math pays off fastest (S2: 2028-29). Storm-time forecast skill stays bound by driver data (Bz).

bottlenecks.name: Radiation belts, energetic particles and spacecraft charging
bottlenecks.description: MeV electron enhancements cause deep-dielectric charging; GEO satellites and EP orbit-raisers spend months in the belts. ML now forecasts alert-level flux crossings up to a week ahead (COVEN, 2026) and charging codes (SPIS, NASCAP-2K) are mature.
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Incremental and expert-scarce: coupling ML forecasts to physics-based radial-diffusion models and calibrating their probabilities. Low novelty; adoption and the conservatism of worst-case design standards bind.

bottlenecks.name: Fusion confinement physics and device engineering (as the basis for fusion propulsion)
bottlenecks.description: Fusion design spends its modeling effort on turbulent transport (a multiscale nonlinear gyrokinetic run can take ~640,000 node-hours), MHD stability and fast-ion confinement, now increasingly through millisecond ML surrogates (Sep 2026). No magnetic device has reached Q > 1, SPARC's first plasma is slipping to 2027, and D-He3 burn, the fuel most propulsion concepts assume, has not been demonstrated.
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Design and surrogate work is expert-scarce and compresses fast (closed-loop stellarator design by ~2029 in S2), but the binding gates are building and operating devices, fuel (He-3) and flight specific power. AI mathematics does not move fusion propulsion inside 2031.

plasma.scenario_contrast: Of the 30 plasma nodes, 11 are first credibly reached by end-2031 in S1, 22 in S2 and 25 in S3; 2031 bands shift from 2 High / 8 Medium / 13 Low / 7 Speculative (S1) to 9/9/9/3 (S2) and 10/12/5/3 (S3). The exponential premise acts almost entirely on the cognitive clock: for tier 2-4 nodes (kinetic solvers, data assimilation, closures, density UQ, design tools) S2 pulls first achievement forward a median ~2 years versus S1 and S3 adds about one more year. From tier 5 down the shift collapses to 0-1 year, because the binding gates become validation campaigns, builds and rideshares (AI-designed thruster: >2031 in S2, 2031 in S3), wall-clock wear testing (23,000 h = 2.6 years), regulator acceptance of model-based life credit, observatories (Vigil launches 2031) and fusion hardware. Mission-level nodes (fusion thrust in space, MW nuclear-electric cargo to Mars, active crew shielding) stay beyond 2031 and Speculative in all three scenarios. S3's recursion mostly helps nodes gated by experiment campaigns that autonomous labs can run (closures, nozzle theory) and barely touches fabrication-, capital- or observation-gated nodes. Shifts for nodes marked '>2031' in S1 are understated because '>2031' is scored as 2032. Upstream shared-node years assumed for consistency: cap-research-math-public 2028/2027/2027; cap-applied-math 2029/2028/2027; cap-physics-theory >2031/2029/2028; cap-design-optimization 2030/2029/2028; infra-mathlib-applied 2030/2028/2027; infra-verified-numerics 2030/2028/2028; infra-tool-qualification >2031/2030/2029; verif-independent-check 2027 in all. If the capability team sets these later, the dependent plasma nodes move by the same amount.
key_insights: The domain's hardest mathematics is not a conjecture. The 60-year Hall-thruster anomalous-transport closure, magnetic-nozzle detachment and space-weather data assimilation are physics-and-numerics problems; the catalog touches the domain directly only through family 362 (Vlasov-Maxwell global smoothness, T3), which is a confidence result.

Under S2 the cognitive bottleneck in electric propulsion (whole-device kinetic simulation, then closure theory) plausibly breaks in 2028-30, but design-before-build thrusters arrive ~2030 and the first AI-designed thruster flies ~2032, because validation campaigns, builds and rideshares bind. The gain shows up first as fewer build-test iterations, not better thrusters.

The fastest real payoff is in drag: thousands of GNSS-tracked constellation satellites are already drag sensors, and turning them into calibrated density products is solved-in-principle estimation theory that on-demand AI makes routine (S2: density UQ 2029, storm-robust operations 2030). The gates are access to proprietary ephemerides and storm-time driver forecasts.

Space-weather skill is input-limited: CME arrival error has sat near 13 h for 11 years and Bz is known only ~30-60 minutes ahead. AI mathematics can plausibly take arrival error toward ~8-10 h by 2030 in S2, but day-ahead Bz needs observatories that will not be operating by 2031.

High-power EP is governed by physical-clock arithmetic: a 23,000-hour life requirement is 2.6 years of continuous firing. The only lever is model-based life credit, which needs regulator acceptance (band capped at Medium) and lands 2030-31 even in S2/S3.

Fusion propulsion timelines are unchanged inside 2031 in every scenario. AI accelerates fusion design (millisecond turbulence surrogates already exist; closed-loop stellarator design ~2029 in S2) but not heating, net gain, D-He3 burn (~50 kg of He-3 per GW-year of fusion power against terrestrial supply of order kilograms per year) or flight-mass devices.

Formalizing plasma kinetic theory has become cheap (a Vlasov-Maxwell-Landau theorem in 10 days for ~$200), so 362's move from T3 to T4 is likely in 2027; the gate is definition alignment in the statement audit, not proof search. Its practical channel is unconditional convergence proofs for kinetic solvers (P2/P6, ~2029 in S2), not device performance.

Scenario sensitivity: S2 doubles the nodes reached by 2031 relative to S1 (11 -> 22 of 30), almost entirely in tiers 2-4 and in data-gated tier-6 forecasting services; S3 adds only three more, because beyond tier 4 the binding gates are physical.
nil_effects: Fusion-powered thrust in space by 2031: no, in any scenario. Net gain, D-He3 burn, He-3 supply, flight specific power and launch approval are physical, fuel and regulatory gates.
Megawatt nuclear-electric cargo to Mars by 2031: no. Needs a flight reactor or MW arrays, space-reactor launch approval and multi-year thruster life tests.
Thruster performance (Isp, efficiency, life) from any catalog theorem: none. 362 (Vlasov-Maxwell) and 363/364 (Boltzmann) are model-confidence results (P5), per analyst position (d).

Galactic speedups do nothing for plasma codes: 107 (matrix multiplication exponent) and 130 (FFT below n log n) leave spectral and PIC solvers on practical FFTs and BLAS. 376 (universal computation in forced Navier-Stokes) and the Sep 8 forced-blowup claim do not bear on plasma or thermosphere modeling practice.

EP system-level limits: propellant supply and price (xenon, krypton, argon), power-processing-unit mass, solar-array specific power and thruster production rate at constellation scale are physics, materials and manufacturing questions.
Day-ahead CME magnetic orientation (Bz) without new observatories: not achievable; the limit is information, not mathematics.
Active radiation-shield mass: the field-length product needed to deflect GeV cosmic rays sets a mass floor that optimization trims but cannot remove.
Wall-clock test durations (thousands of hours of wear testing, D-T campaigns) do not compress with cognition; only regulator-accepted model credit can shorten them.

Validation opportunities for storm-time models: Solar Cycle 25 peaked in Oct 2024 and declines to ~2030, so fewer extreme storms are available before 2031 to validate improved density and forecast models (strong declining-phase events still occur).

signposts.what_it_changes: Unlocks plasma-ep-life-by-analysis and the EP cycle-time outcome; refusal confines AI gains to design, not qualification.

prop.domain: Chemical and nuclear-thermal propulsion, fluids and combustion

bottlenecks.name: Turbulence and turbulent-combustion modeling (closure error and CFD cost)
bottlenecks.description: Wall heat flux for regenerative cooling, propellant mixing, nozzle separation and injector flow all ride on turbulence closures. RANS cannot reliably predict separated flows (CFD Vision 2030 reviews); ML closures often fail to generalize (JFM 2025; arXiv 2604.25824). LES at engine conditions is prohibitively expensive (JAXA 2025), and stiff chemistry dominates reacting-flow cost: one LES realization of 2 ms of a spray with a 54-species mechanism took 48,000 core-hours and up to 20 days (UConn 2023). Exascale runs reach 60 billion cells (Pele on Frontier) and still cannot do engine-scale DNS.
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Mixed. Genuinely open: closures that generalize and a convergence theory for LES (prop-closure-theory, prop-les-convergence-theory). Solved in principle but scarce experts or labor: certified reduced chemistry, solution verification and UQ (prop-stiff-chemistry, prop-cfd-auto-vv), where on-demand AI is the unlock. Navier–Stokes regularity is irrelevant here (P5, nil). For the open part, data binds, not cognition.

bottlenecks.name: Combustion dynamics: thermoacoustic instability, ignition and relight, detonation-engine wave modes
bottlenecks.description: Instability is still found and fixed on the test stand. The F-1's 'Project Go' ran 2,000 tests on 210 injector designs (enginehistory.org). Network models now predict acoustic frequencies within <5% (de Jong Cantarino et al. 2026), but growth rates and triggering depend on flame response at 100-350 bar, which is not predictable. In 2026 Starship showed live transient problems: Raptor 3 shutdowns <20 s into boostback (Flight 12) and only 10 of 13 booster engines relighting on Flight 13 (Jul 25, 2026). RDRE wave-mode bifurcation and injector coupling are open research while NASA hardware runs 340-s firings.
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Stability certificates and bifurcation analysis of reduced models are expert-scarce applied math, the clearest P1 win (prop-certified-stability-rom: High by 2031 in S2). Flame response and RDE mode theory are open physics problems that need experiments (Medium in S2).

bottlenecks.name: Cryogenic fluid management in microgravity (boil-off, self-pressurization, slosh, chilldown, transfer, gauging)
bottlenecks.description: The critical path for Starship HLS: NASA OIG (Mar 2026) calls cryogenic transfer 'one of the most significant technical challenges'; tanker estimates range from SpaceX's '10-ish' to NASA's 'high teens'. Even in 1 g, NASA's validated CFD ranges from within 3% (laminar) to 15-16% under-prediction of tank pressure and up to 40% error on vapor temperature (k-omega SST), hinging on a tuned evaporation coefficient (Kartuzova et al., SciTech 2025). Microgravity flight data are scarce.
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Mostly data-limited. Once Starship transfer and LOXSAT flight data exist, calibration and uncertainty analysis are routine applied math. Gauging has a genuine inverse-problem component; family 365 (T3) marks a nonuniqueness ceiling.

bottlenecks.name: Engine life, thermomechanical fatigue and reuse
bottlenecks.description: Reuse economics turn on refurbishment intervals. Life prediction is limited by heat-flux uncertainty, plasticity-model choice and lack of specimen data (Lisbon thesis 2024; Polito 2025), with additively-manufactured parts adding scatter. Methods (Morrow, Norton, Miner) rest on SSME-era data.
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Strong. Probabilistic life modeling with UQ is expert-scarce, solved-in-principle applied math (prop-life-twin). Operators already hold fleet data. The heat-flux input inherits the closure problem.

bottlenecks.name: Turbomachinery: cavitation instabilities, rotordynamics, start transients
bottlenecks.description: Rotating cavitation, cavitation surge and rotordynamic instability drive turbopump failures. CFD predictions depend strongly on the cavitation and turbulence model chosen; 3D linear perturbation theories with dynamic transfer matrices are advancing (Pisa thesis 2025). Start and relight sequences are stiff transient systems with uncertain two-phase chilldown physics.
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Stability of transfer-matrix and rotordynamic models is applied math that S2 makes cheap; the cavitation-compliance inputs need rigs and closures.

bottlenecks.name: Verification, validation and credibility of simulation
bottlenecks.description: Code verification, solution verification, UQ and credibility assessment (NASA-STD-7009 style) are known methods that are rarely done in full on engine CFD because they are labor-intensive (general). This is why tests are often run to settle questions a simulation may already have answered.
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: The biggest solved-in-principle-but-expensive category: automated V&V (prop-cfd-auto-vv, P1->P2) and formally verified controller software (prop-verified-engine-software, P2). Certification acceptance gates the credit.

bottlenecks.name: Nuclear thermal propulsion: fuel and materials in hot hydrogen, test infrastructure, policy
bottlenecks.description: Core materials must survive 2,500-3,000 K hydrogen at >3 MPa under irradiation; GA-EMS fuel survived six cycles to 2,600 K (Jan 2025). Neutron transport is mature (general). DRACO was cancelled in 2025 on ROI grounds tied to falling launch costs (Breaking Defense, Jun 27, 2025); Congress put >=$110M into NTP for FY2026, but the April 2026 Space Nuclear Initiative prioritizes NEP (SR-1 Freedom, Mars 2028) and surface power. A ground test needs an exhaust-capture facility (designs exist, NASA 2023).
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Little. The binding gates are irradiation testing, facilities, approvals and money. Catalog links (278, 275, T1) only restate known limits of DFT.

prop.scenario_contrast: The tree compresses from the top. S1 (Plateau): public research-grade math arrives ~2028, AI applied math ~2029-30, and AI physics theory after 2031. Tier-2 nodes (certified stability models, automated V&V, gauging limits, life prediction) land 2029-2030 at Medium. Tier-3 physics nodes (closures, flame response, plume–surface interaction, NTP fuels) mostly slip past 2031. Tier 5-6 nodes run on their physical clocks: transfer demo 2027, HLS refueling 2029, RDE in-space demo 2029. S2 (Exponential, base case): tier-2 nodes pull forward 1-2 years to 2027-2028 and reach High. Tier-3 physics nodes arrive 2028-2030 but stay Medium, because high-pressure reacting data, microgravity flight data and irradiation data bind once theory is cheap. Tier-4 tools land 2028-2030. Tier 5-6 nodes move 0-1 year, because launch cadence, test stands, qualification and appropriations bind, and tier-7 outcomes mostly land after 2031. S3 (Recursive): autonomous labs and AI-accelerated hardware iteration pull experiment-gated nodes a further ~1 year (flame response, RDE, NTP fuel model) and lift HLS refueling to High. Irradiation time, nuclear approvals, NTP capital and the statistics of reliability demonstration (~230 zero-failure tests for 0.99 at 90% confidence) do not compress. Between S1 and S2, the median cognitive node (tiers 1-3) moves ~2 years earlier and the median physical node (tiers 5-6) about 0 years. Shared upstream years assumed here: cap-research-math-public S1 2028 / S2 2027 / S3 2027; cap-applied-math 2029 / 2027 / 2027; cap-physics-theory >2031 / 2028 / 2028; cap-design-optimization 2030 / 2028 / 2028; cap-autonomous-labs >2031 / 2029 / 2028; infra-verified-numerics 2030 / 2028 / 2028; infra-tool-qualification >2031 / 2030 / 2029; verif-independent-check 2027 in all three.
key_insights: Propulsion is bound by physical clocks. Under the exponential base case (S2), cognitive nodes (tiers 1-3) arrive ~2 years earlier than under the plateau, while flight and mission nodes (tiers 5-6) move by 0-1 year, because launch cadence, test stands, qualification, irradiation time and appropriations bind.

Navier–Stokes is a dead end for propulsion engineering. The Sep 8, 2026 forced-blowup claim (T3, unreviewed) and even a future resolution of the unforced Clay problem change confidence in the equations, not codes, closures or engines. An independent analysis (arXiv 2609.17642) finds the mechanism unreachable in buildable flows. The paper should say this plainly, because readers will assume the opposite.

The largest near-term gains are in expert-scarce work that is solved in principle: certified combustion-stability margins for reduced models, automated CFD verification and UQ, probabilistic engine-life prediction and gauging analysis. All travel P1, and all are High by 2031 under S2. The catalog contributes little here; the capability does (position a).

Where the physics is genuinely open (turbulence and combustion closures, flame response at 100-350 bar, microgravity cryogenics, plume–surface interaction), cheap theory meets a data wall. Under S2 the binding gate shifts from cognition to data, and the most valuable assets become data generators: Starship transfer flights, LOXSAT, high-pressure combustion rigs and vacuum-chamber plume tests.

Better boil-off models are worth more the slower the launch cadence. In an illustrative 1,200 t depot fill with 120 t tankers, boil-off of 0.05-0.3%/day costs ~1 extra tanker at one launch per 6 days but 3-5 extra at one per 12 days with 0.3-0.5%/day. Validated cryogenic models are worth ~1-4 tankers per HLS-class mission, roughly 10-30% of campaign launches.

Models cut redesign loops, not reliability demonstration. Showing 0.99 reliability at 90% confidence still takes ~230 zero-failure tests unless customers accept model-based Bayesian credit, so engine-development compression by 2031 is Low even in S2. The lever is a rule change, not a theorem.

Nuclear thermal propulsion is gated by policy and capital, not mathematics. DRACO died on ROI as launch costs fell; FY2026 holds only ~$110M; the April 2026 initiative prioritizes NEP. An NTP ground test by 2031 is Low and a crewed Mars NTP stage is Speculative in every scenario.

Catalog links to this domain are thin and mostly conditional. Families 376, 149, 363, 364, 278, 275, 372 and 366 are T1. Only 143 (limit cycles) and 365 (boundary-data nonuniqueness for gauging) are T3, and both are marginal: one bounds oscillation states with no practical constant, the other marks a ceiling on tomographic gauging.
nil_effects: Navier–Stokes regularity, forced or unforced: no change to CFD codes, turbulence closures, injector design or test plans. Effect is P5 confidence only, and real flows cavitate, shock or leave the continuum regime before any singularity matters.
The galactic algorithm results in the release (matrix-multiplication exponent, sub-n log n FFT) do not make CFD, LES or chemistry solvers faster in practice (position e).
Thermochemical Isp ceilings: LOX/CH4 (~380 s vacuum) and LOX/LH2 (~460 s) are fixed by propellant thermochemistry (general). No mathematics raises them; only new propellants or nuclear heating do.

Qualification physics and statistics: bomb tests, duration tests and reliability demonstration (~230 zero-failure tests for 0.99 at 90% confidence) are unchanged unless customers and regulators accept model-based credit.
Launch cadence and tanker count: HLS refueling timing is set by vehicle reliability, pads and flight rate. Better models move it by months at most.
NTP gates: irradiation time to accumulate fluence, HALEU supply, an exhaust-capture test facility, nuclear safety and launch approvals, and appropriations are untouched by AI math.

Solid rocket motors: the constraint is energetics and chemical supply chains and factory capacity (Anduril targets 6,000 tactical motors/yr by end-2026; Raytheon reports motor supply still constrains output), not modeling.

Materials limits: copper-alloy liner temperature, hydrogen attack on fuels and turbine materials, and additive-manufacturing defect scatter are physics and process problems. The DFT ceilings in families 278 and 275 (T1) do not change materials practice.

science.domain: Space science, fundamental physics and exotic-propulsion ceilings

bottlenecks.name: Forward models of the sources
bottlenecks.description: Predicting what an instrument should see: gravitational waveforms (numerical relativity, gravitational self-force), exoplanet atmosphere and molecular-opacity models, coronal and solar-wind models, cosmological simulations. Errors here become biased science: LISA studies show neglected higher harmonics or eccentricity bias massive-black-hole parameters at SNRs in the hundreds to thousands, and JWST retrievals of the same spectrum give disparate answers.
bottlenecks.share_of_effort: ~30% of modeling and analysis effort in the domain (analyst judgment)
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: High where the work is expert-scarce derivation plus code: second-order self-force on spinning black holes, well-posedness of beyond-Einstein gravity, error-controlled waveform surrogates. Under S2 these 5-8 year programs could compress to 2-3 years. Low where lab data or compute binds: opacities need laboratory spectroscopy, LISA-grade numerical relativity needs supercomputer time.

bottlenecks.name: Inverse problems and inference at scale
bottlenecks.description: Turning data into parameters with honest uncertainty: LISA's 'global fit' of tens of thousands of overlapping signals, exoplanet atmospheric retrievals, simulation-based cosmological inference for DESI, Euclid, Rubin and Roman, sparse-aperture VLBI imaging (EHT, BHEX), 3D heliospheric tomography from a few viewpoints (PUNCH).
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: High and fast: identifiability and stability theorems (what a dataset can and cannot determine), calibrated inference with coverage guarantees, certified emulators. Mostly P3/P5 within 1-3 years with no hardware needed; collaboration adoption is the gate. Mostly 'solved in principle but expert-scarce' rather than famous open problems.

bottlenecks.name: Instrument stability and integrated modeling
bottlenecks.description: Closing error budgets for extreme instruments: HWO needs raw contrast ~1e-10, 1-sigma photometric precision ~3e-12 and contrast drift of order 1e-11 to 1e-10 during observations, which means picometer-class wavefront stability; LISA needs drag-free control and picometer interferometry; space clocks and atom interferometers need full systematic-error models.
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Medium: provable coronagraph throughput limits, wavefront controllers with convergence and robustness guarantees, AI-run integrated structural-thermal-optical models. But testbeds, deformable mirrors, detectors and thermal hardware set achieved performance, and testbed time is scarce.

bottlenecks.name: Data supply: photons, missions, downlink and lab measurements
bottlenecks.description: Most open science questions in the domain (is dark energy evolving, is a gas biological, why is the corona hot) are data-limited. Mission count is set by budgets: NASA's FY2026 budget is $24.4B and the FY2027 request is $18.8B. Laboratory opacities and reaction rates are a separate, slow data supply.
bottlenecks.share_of_effort: ~15% of effort, but the dominant binding constraint
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Low: optimal experimental design and better target selection squeeze more from each photon but cannot create data. Autonomous labs (S2/S3) can speed laboratory spectroscopy and chemical kinetics.

bottlenecks.name: Credibility of extraordinary claims
bottlenecks.description: Checking biosignature detections (the K2-18 b dimethyl-sulfide debate), dark-energy anomalies, new-physics hints and exotic-propulsion proposals. Today small groups do this over months to years: Lentz's 2020 positive-energy warp claim was shown to violate the weak energy condition only in Nov 2025.
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: High and fast (P3): independent AI re-analysis within weeks; certified checks (interval-arithmetic energy-condition tests for warp metrics already exist). Limits: reviewer attention and formal libraries; Mathlib has essentially no Lorentzian geometry, so GR claims cannot yet be Lean-checked (general).

bottlenecks.name: Programmatics: flagship schedules and budgets
bottlenecks.description: LISA launches in 2035; HWO in the 2040s; small missions need competitive selection (BHEX plans a 2026 Small Explorer proposal and a 2031 launch). These dates set when any math-enabled capability can fly.
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Nil on dates. Indirect only: cheaper design closure and stronger proposals.

science.scenario_contrast: S1 (plateau): research-grade AI mathematics reaches outside teams around 2027-28 but stays strongest in pure mathematics; the domain gets fast ceilings (warp no-go theorems, coronagraph and interferometry identifiability limits, claim audits) and an archival-analysis boost, while LISA's self-force program, LISA-grade numerical relativity and biosignature theory finish on roughly their pre-AI schedules (after 2031). S2 (exponential, base case): applied math is routine by 2027-28 and physics theory by 2028-29, so the expert-scarce theory backlog collapses: second-order self-force in Kerr by ~2029 (four to six years early), LISA analysis readiness by ~2030, retrieval identifiability and certified cosmological inference by 2028, quantified biosignature false-positive maps by ~2030 and AI-closed HWO requirements by ~2030. Yet no flight date moves: LISA still launches in 2035, HWO in the 2040s, BHEX no earlier than 2031, and dark-energy and biosignature questions wait for photons. S3 (recursive) pulls the cognitive nodes forward another year and raises bands on theory-heavy items (beyond-GR well-posedness, coronal heating), but compute (numerical relativity), laboratory validation (opacities), qualification (quantum sensors) and capital (BHEX, HWO, lightsail demos) bind just as hard. The domain's signature is a widening gap between theory readiness and data arrival: by 2031 under S2, space science is limited by photons, downlink and budgets rather than by analysis.
key_insights: In space science AI mathematics changes the cognitive half of a mission (theory, waveforms, inference, design closure) and none of the flight dates: LISA 2035, HWO 2040s and BHEX no earlier than 2031 in every scenario.

The highest-leverage targets are expert-scarce applied problems, not famous conjectures: second-order self-force around spinning black holes is done today only for circular orbits around non-spinning ones; under S2 it could finish around 2029, four to six years ahead of the pre-AI path, turning LISA's extreme-mass-ratio science from a risk into a baseline.

The catalog's GR results are science-only. Family 264 (strong cosmic censorship near Kerr) has zero mission relevance; family 260 (spacetime Penrose inequalities) is T1 for its main inequalities. Only a supporting construction has unchecked Lean, and the repo's own Lean doc says the general inequality is unformalized. Both raise confidence (P5); neither changes a model.

For exotic propulsion AI mathematics can only deliver ceilings, and the ceilings were mostly in place before AI: the null-energy theorem (2021) and positive mass (1979-81). What is new is sharpness and auditing at scale: the Sep 2026 Natario result shows negative energy grows as R^4/Delta^3, so halving a bubble wall costs 8x more. The effect is to redirect a tiny funding pool, not to enable anything.

Where AI mathematics enables in this domain, it does so through inverse-problem theory feeding instrument design: coronagraph throughput limits, space-VLBI identifiability, heliospheric tomography uniqueness, quantum-sensor error budgets. These act within 1-3 years (P3/P5) and inform designs frozen in 2027-30, but fly after 2031.

Data-bound questions (is dark energy evolving, is a gas biological, Hubble tension) are not settled by mathematics; AI shortens analysis lag by about a year and makes claims more credible, but photons bind.

The main 2031 outcome is more science per mission dollar from public archives, a High-band effect in S2 because nothing physical gates it, set against a NASA budget request 23% lower for FY2027 than FY2026's enacted level.

General relativity is a formalization desert: Mathlib has essentially no Lorentzian geometry, so GR results will stay at T1-T3 longer than discrete mathematics, and certified warp-drive audits will rely on interval arithmetic before Lean.
nil_effects: Launch and flight dates: LISA (2035), HWO (2040s) and BHEX (2031 at earliest) do not move in any scenario; capital, fabrication, qualification and launch bind.
No warp drive, reactionless drive or traversable wormhole becomes possible; AI mathematics can only tighten no-go bounds (ceilings, P3).
Strong cosmic censorship near Kerr (264) has no mission or engineering implication.
Photon-limited questions (5-sigma dark-energy evolution, Hubble tension, a biosignature on a specific planet) are gated by survey and telescope data, not mathematics.

The galactic matrix-multiplication and FFT bounds in the release do not speed up cosmology, gravitational-wave or imaging pipelines (tl-position-1); log-concave sampling (139) is theory-only for real multimodal posteriors.
Angular resolution of space VLBI is set by baseline length over wavelength and coronagraph contrast by diffraction, wavefront stability and photon noise; theorems define limits, not new physics.
Quantum-sensor sensitivity in orbit is hardware-limited (lasers, vacuum, atom sources); laboratory spectroscopy, vacuum testbeds and supercomputer time do not compress with cognition.
The catalog's elliptic inverse-problem results (365, 372) do not apply to Fourier-sampled interferometric imaging or line-of-sight tomography.
