materials-microgravity-process-models.title: Knowing what is worth making in orbit
materials-microgravity-process-models.description: Validated models of microgravity processing (ZBLAN fiber crystallization; vapor-phase growth of GaN, SiC, AlN and diamond; pharmaceutical crystallization) that quantify the quality gain over the best terrestrial processes and predict which products justify launch and return.
materials-microgravity-process-models.status_oct2026: Flawless Photonics drew ~12 km of ZBLAN fiber on the ISS (2024; longest continuous length 1,141 m) with lower attenuation than ground-drawn fiber; Space Forge's ForgeStar-1 generated ~1,000 C plasma more than 100 times from Dec 2025 for wide-bandgap crystal growth; Varda re-entered capsules W-5 (Jan 2026) and W-6 (May 2026).
materials-microgravity-process-models.why: The in-space-manufacturing business case turns on a quantitative quality gain (defect density, optical attenuation) over terrestrial best practice. Models of convection suppression, nucleation and transport are applied math that AI can do on demand; validation data come from a handful of flights a year, which binds.
materials-microgravity-process-models.strongest_case_small: Terrestrial processes keep improving and may erase the microgravity advantage; launch, return and volume economics dominate over physics knowledge.
materials-microgravity-process-models.signpost: Space Forge or Flawless Photonics publishes measured defect-density or attenuation advantages for a sellable product, with a model that predicted the gain, by 2028.

materials-ht-alloy-design.title: AI designs new rocket-engine alloys in weeks
materials-ht-alloy-design.description: AI agents run the full integrated computational materials engineering (ICME) loop (composition, phase stability, printability, heat treatment, predicted creep, oxidation and hydrogen resistance) for printed high-temperature alloys, with a high hit rate on first validation coupons.
materials-ht-alloy-design.status_oct2026: Human-led ICME is already fast: GRX-810's composition was set by thermodynamic modeling in weeks rather than years (NASA, 2022); a NASA burn-resistant alloy went from concept to test specimens in about three months (AMAA, Jul 2026); QuesTek's Ferrium M54 was designed in under a year. DARPA's METALS program funds multi-objective alloy-and-structure design.
materials-ht-alloy-design.why: Design is already the short pole (weeks to months); AI agents push it toward days and widen the search to multi-principal-element and oxide-dispersion-strengthened chemistries tuned for printability. The value is hit rate: fewer failed powder lots and builds, each a months-long physical cycle. Validation coupons, creep tests and hot-fire bind.
materials-ht-alloy-design.strongest_case_small: Design time is already a small share of the 6-20-year insertion timeline, so compressing it further saves little calendar time on its own.
materials-ht-alloy-design.signpost: An engine maker or NASA announces an AI-agent-designed alloy entering AMRL 4-5 (parameter development and property characterization) by 2028.

materials-uhtc-tps-design.title: AI-designed heat shields and hot structures
materials-uhtc-tps-design.description: Computational design of ultra-high-temperature ceramics, high-entropy carbides and borides, ceramic-matrix composites and ablators, with predicted oxidation, ablation and fracture behaviour for reentry and hypersonic thermal protection systems (TPS).
materials-uhtc-tps-design.status_oct2026: AI-driven, high-throughput design of ultra-high-temperature high-entropy ceramics is an active field (Engineering, 2026); ML-accelerated simulations have predicted high-entropy carbides melting above ~4,400 K (general). Varda manufactures C-PICA heat shields in-house. 366 (Mumford-Shah planar crack regularity, T1) touches the variational theory behind phase-field fracture models.
materials-uhtc-tps-design.why: TPS performance is set by surface chemistry (oxide-scale formation and volatilization above ~1,800 C), ablation kinetics and thermal-shock fracture, each a multiphysics model AI can build and optimize. Arc-jet and plasma-torch test capacity binds (general). 366 raises confidence that the phase-field fracture models used for ceramic cracking approximate a well-behaved limit in 2D (P5, small).
materials-uhtc-tps-design.strongest_case_small: Reusable-TPS gains often come from manufacturing, attachment and inspection (tile gaps, bonding), not chemistry, and arc-jet facility time is scarce.
materials-uhtc-tps-design.signpost: A new AI-designed ultra-high-temperature ceramic or ablator tested in an arc jet with performance matching pre-test predictions, by 2028.

materials-energetics-design.title: AI-designed green and high-energy propellants
materials-energetics-design.description: Multi-objective molecular and formulation design of propellants that jointly predicts performance (specific impulse, density), sensitivity, thermal stability, toxicity and synthesizability, closing the loop with automated small-scale synthesis.
materials-energetics-design.status_oct2026: Machine learning plus genetic algorithms screened >1,000 candidates down to 7 energetic compounds with predicted specific impulse up to 278 s for solid propellants (NWPU); transfer-learned message-passing networks predict impact sensitivity and vapour pressure from small datasets (UC Irvine seminar, Mar 2026). 149 (T1, permanence of weakly reversible reaction networks) concerns the qualitative behaviour of mass-action kinetics.
materials-energetics-design.why: Propellant design is a constrained multi-objective search in which sensitivity and stability, not specific impulse, eliminate most candidates. Better electronic-structure accuracy improves decomposition-barrier and heat-of-formation predictions; autonomous microsynthesis supplies data. Synthesis and hazard testing in the few labs licensed for energetics bind.
materials-energetics-design.strongest_case_small: Chemical propellants sit near thermochemical ceilings; realistic gains are handling, toxicity and density worth single-digit percent; 149's qualitative kinetics result changes no practice.
materials-energetics-design.signpost: An AI-designed energetic molecule synthesized and hazard-tested with measured sensitivity matching prediction, by 2028.

materials-am-digital-twin-qual.title: Certify each printed part from its build data
materials-am-digital-twin-qual.description: In-situ monitoring plus a validated physics/ML digital twin certifies each printed part ('print and fly') with reduced CT and witness testing, accepted first for non-fracture-critical and then for fracture-critical spaceflight hardware.
materials-am-digital-twin-qual.status_oct2026: Described as the ideal end-state in 2026 TMS and ASME qualification work; NASA-STD-6030 requires per-machine qualification and statistical process control; no regulator credit for twin-based part certification of the most critical hardware as of Oct 2026. 372 (T1: smooth isotropic Lame moduli are uniquely determined by boundary data) and 365 (T3: joint metric and connection recovery, plus conductivity nonuniqueness) bear on full-field nondestructive evaluation.
materials-am-digital-twin-qual.premise_tier: T1 (372); T3 (365); both peripheral to the main chain
materials-am-digital-twin-qual.why: Inspection, witness coupons and proof testing are a large share of the cost and schedule of the most critical printed parts (general). If the defect-physics model predicts part life from sensor data, CT can be targeted and lot testing shrinks. 372 supports that elastic property maps are identifiable from boundary measurements (P5); 365's conductivity nonuniqueness marks where eddy-current or impedance inspection cannot uniquely locate anomalies (P3). Acceptance by NASA and customers binds; band capped at Medium.
materials-am-digital-twin-qual.strongest_case_small: For fracture-critical engine parts, programs will demand physical evidence for years, so first credit will be partial (less critical parts); uniqueness theorems (372, 365) say nothing about stability under noise, which is the practical inspection limit.
materials-am-digital-twin-qual.signpost: NASA, the FAA or a launch provider grants formal credit for in-situ-monitoring-based acceptance of a flight part, by 2029.

materials-verified-fault-tolerance.title: Proven radiation-fault tolerance for orbital AI
materials-verified-fault-tolerance.description: Machine-checked proofs that fault-tolerance layers (error-correcting codes, memory scrubbing, checkpointing, algorithm-based fault tolerance for matrix operations, voting logic) bound the probability of undetected errors under a stated radiation fault model.
materials-verified-fault-tolerance.status_oct2026: Fault tolerance for commercial chips in space is designed with margins and tested empirically. Agentic Lean formalization exists (127 families in the release carry Lean proofs) but verified floating-point and numerics toolchains are immature. No catalog family addresses this.
materials-verified-fault-tolerance.why: Formal verification is the bridge to safety-critical use. Here the property is crisp (for example, a checksum-protected matrix multiply detects any single-bit fault with probability at least 1 - 1e-9) and the systems are commercial, so no regulator gate binds. Proven bounds let operators choose light mitigation with confidence, capturing the ~2.5x compute-per-watt lever in the radiation-error node.
materials-verified-fault-tolerance.strongest_case_small: Proofs are only as good as the fault model: multi-bit upsets, latch-ups and memory-controller failures may fall outside it, and operators may trust empirical flight data over proofs.
materials-verified-fault-tolerance.signpost: An orbital-compute operator or Nvidia publishes a verified algorithm-based-fault-tolerance or error-correction library used in flight, by 2028.

materials-battery-life-qual.title: Battery qualification without years of cycling
materials-battery-life-qual.description: Physics-based and data-driven degradation models (solid-electrolyte-interphase growth, lithium plating, silicon-anode swelling, solid-state interfaces) that predict end-of-life capacity under low-Earth-orbit cycling from early-cycle data, with validated uncertainty.
materials-battery-life-qual.status_oct2026: ISRO qualified 10 Ah silicon-graphite cells at 190 Wh/kg (versus 157 Wh/kg) with a Jan 2024 flight demonstration and expects 35-40% battery mass saving; JAXA is testing an all-solid-state battery on the ISS. Low-Earth-orbit cycling at ~15 orbits/day means ~5,500 cycles a year and ~27,000 over five years (general).
materials-battery-life-qual.why: Life testing at orbital cadence takes years, and accelerated cycling changes degradation mechanisms, so new chemistries (silicon anodes, solid state) wait for real-time data. Validated early-life prediction could cut qualification life testing from ~3-5 years to ~1-2 (assumption), letting electric-vehicle cell gains reach spacecraft sooner.
materials-battery-life-qual.strongest_case_small: Battery progress is driven by the electric-vehicle industry, and constellations already fly screened commercial cells; the space-specific contribution of AI math is small.
materials-battery-life-qual.signpost: A space battery supplier qualifies a new cell chemistry using model-based life prediction with reduced real-time cycling, by 2029.

materials-closed-loop-discovery.title: Autonomous labs discover real new materials
materials-closed-loop-discovery.description: AI-run labs deliver independently replicated new functional materials (PV absorbers, coatings, electrolytes, catalysts, alloys) at more than ten times the human discovery rate.
materials-closed-loop-discovery.status_oct2026: Periodic Labs ($300M seed, Sep 2025; superconductors as its north star), Lila Sciences (~$450M raised; 'hundreds of thousands' of AI-driven experiments in catalysts, thin films and ultra-stable metals) and Google DeepMind's UK automated lab (announced Dec 2025, opening 2026, planning hundreds of materials per day). No independently replicated space-relevant discovery found as of Oct 2026.
materials-closed-loop-discovery.why: Robotic powder synthesis is now cheap and repeatable; with reliable characterization and trustworthy screening, discovery rates can rise roughly tenfold. For space, the first beneficiaries are materials made by simple routes (PV absorbers, coatings, electrolytes), not superalloys or ceramic composites whose processing autonomous labs cannot yet do.
materials-closed-loop-discovery.strongest_case_small: Discovery is not space's bottleneck; insertion is (more than 20 years and ~$400M for aerospace materials by Materials Genome Initiative-era estimates). More candidates only lengthen the qualification queue.
materials-closed-loop-discovery.signpost: The first independently replicated discovery from Periodic Labs, Lila or DeepMind's UK lab, with full characterization, by end-2027.

materials-ai-alloy-flight.title: First AI-designed alloy flies in a rocket engine
materials-ai-alloy-flight.description: An alloy whose composition was primarily proposed by an AI design system flies in flight hardware (combustion chamber, preburner, turbine or nozzle) on a commercial launch vehicle or spacecraft.
materials-ai-alloy-flight.status_oct2026: No AI-designed alloy has flown (general). Benchmarks: the GRCop family was developed in 1987 and its printed variant GRCop-42 flew on Relativity's Terran 1 in 2023, about eight years after AM work began (~2015); Ferrium M54 went from design to flight qualification in under six years; GRX-810 (2022) and NASA HR-1 are still maturing.
materials-ai-alloy-flight.why: With design compressed to weeks (S2, from 2028), the floor is physical: powder atomization lots, parameter development, property testing and hot-fire campaigns, roughly 2-3 years for a risk-tolerant commercial engine maker that certifies its own hardware. Value: hotter preburners and turbines and longer-life chambers for reusable engines.
materials-ai-alloy-flight.strongest_case_small: Primes stick with heritage alloys (Inconel 718, GRCop) because supply chains and data exist; NASA's AMRL framework notes high alloy maturity is not a qualified material; S3's faster cognition cannot speed up hot-fire testing.
materials-ai-alloy-flight.signpost: An AI-designed alloy enters hot-fire testing at SpaceX, Relativity, Ursa Major or NASA Marshall by 2028.

materials-tps-new-material-flight.title: AI-designed heat-shield material flies
materials-tps-new-material-flight.description: An AI-designed thermal-protection material, coating or ablator flies on a reentry vehicle, first as an instrumented test coupon on a commercial capsule and then as a primary heat-shield zone.
materials-tps-new-material-flight.status_oct2026: Varda's W-5 (Jan 2026) and W-6 (May 2026) capsules re-entered with in-house C-PICA heat shields, a cadence of one reentry every few months; no AI-designed TPS material has flown (general).
materials-tps-new-material-flight.why: Commercial capsules turn flight testing from a once-a-decade event into a quarterly one, a physical-gate compression independent of AI, so a coupon of an AI-designed ceramic or ablator could fly within about a year of arc-jet screening.
materials-tps-new-material-flight.strongest_case_small: Flying a coupon is not adoption: crewed and large reusable vehicles demand years of arc-jet data and flight heritage.
materials-tps-new-material-flight.signpost: A capsule operator announces a flight experiment of an AI-designed TPS coupon, by 2028.

materials-perovskite-tandem-flight.title: Model-qualified perovskite tandem proves itself in orbit
materials-perovskite-tandem-flight.description: A perovskite tandem (on silicon, CIGS or III-V) whose composition and encapsulation were optimized with validated degradation models completes at least one year in low Earth orbit with under 10% relative power loss, as predicted. Non-AI perovskite demonstrations continue regardless; this node is the model-qualified version.
materials-perovskite-tandem-flight.status_oct2026: Perovskite tandems in orbit since Jul 2024 (Potsdam/HZB); RIT CubeSat test; certified 27.49% AM0 tandem with balloon flight (Aug 2026). No published one-year on-orbit stability record with a predictive model found as of Oct 2026.
materials-perovskite-tandem-flight.why: Perovskite tandems could beat III-V multijunction cells on cost per watt and specific power, but only on-orbit exposure validates lifetime: models from 2028 (S2), cells flown 2029, one year of data by 2030. S3 cannot compress the year in orbit.
materials-perovskite-tandem-flight.strongest_case_small: III-V multijunction cells (commercial >29.5% AM0; 34.2% record triple junction) already serve high-value missions; the perovskite advantage is cost and mass, which matters only at very large array scale.
materials-perovskite-tandem-flight.signpost: Published one-year on-orbit data for any perovskite tandem by 2027-28.

materials-wbg-rad-hard-power.title: Radiation-robust SiC and GaN power electronics
materials-wbg-rad-hard-power.description: Wide-bandgap power transistors with a mechanism-level model of heavy-ion single-event burnout and leakage degradation, redesigned to run near rated voltage in space.
materials-wbg-rad-hard-power.status_oct2026: SiC power MOSFETs and diodes show heavy-ion-induced leakage degradation and single-event burnout well below rated voltage, forcing heavy derating, often to about half of rated voltage or less (general; NASA NEPP work). The physical mechanism is still debated.
materials-wbg-rad-hard-power.why: High-voltage (300-800 V class) buses cut harness mass and losses for 100 kW-class orbital compute and electric propulsion; derating 1,200 V parts to ~50% throws away much of SiC's advantage. Explaining the mechanism (defect physics and impact ionization under ion strikes) is a physics-theory problem; each device redesign then takes about a year per fab cycle plus beam tests, which bind.
materials-wbg-rad-hard-power.strongest_case_small: Vendors may fix it empirically with thicker drift layers and derating; the rad-hard power market is small, so fab priority is low.
materials-wbg-rad-hard-power.signpost: A vendor releases a SiC MOSFET qualified free of single-event burnout at 80% or more of rated voltage under standard heavy-ion testing, by 2029.

materials-new-propellant-flight.title: AI-designed propellant flies
materials-new-propellant-flight.description: A propellant molecule or formulation primarily proposed by an AI design system is qualified and flown in a spacecraft or launch-vehicle propulsion system.
materials-new-propellant-flight.status_oct2026: Benchmark: AFRL's AF-M315E (now ASCENT) originated more than 20 years before NASA's Green Propellant Infusion Mission flew it in Jun 2019. No AI-designed propellant has flown (general).
materials-new-propellant-flight.why: After design (S2, 2028), scale-up synthesis, hazard classification, long-duration materials-compatibility tests, catalyst development and thruster qualification set a ~3-5-year floor even for a startup, longer for NASA or ESA.
materials-new-propellant-flight.strongest_case_small: A few percent of specific impulse or density rarely justifies requalification, and existing green propellants (ASCENT, LMP-103S) already serve the market.
materials-new-propellant-flight.signpost: A propulsion startup announces a thruster qualification program for an AI-designed propellant, by 2029.

materials-cots-orbital-compute-ops.title: Commercial AI chips running in orbit at scale
materials-cots-orbital-compute-ops.description: Operational orbital AI compute (clusters of 100 kW class or more with paying customers) on commercial accelerators, with radiation mitigation sized from validated system-level fault models rather than blanket margins.
materials-cots-orbital-compute-ops.status_oct2026: Starcloud H100 in orbit since Nov 2025; Google/Planet Suncatcher prototypes due by early 2027; Nvidia Space-1 Vera Rubin module targeted for 2027 with six launch partners (Aetherflux, Axiom Space, Kepler, Planet, Sophia Space, Starcloud).
materials-cots-orbital-compute-ops.why: Orbital compute will happen on capital and launch economics; AI math contributes cheaper radiation hardness assurance and lighter mitigation (up to ~2.5x useful compute per watt by using algorithm-based fault tolerance instead of triple redundancy, general), which improves unit economics.
materials-cots-orbital-compute-ops.strongest_case_small: This proceeds whatever happens in AI math; Google's measured dose margins suggest radiation is not the binding constraint in dawn-dusk sun-synchronous orbit, where 33FG estimates ~100 um coverglass and under 1%/yr PV degradation.
materials-cots-orbital-compute-ops.signpost: Paying-customer service from an orbital compute cluster of 100 kW or more, with published radiation-error statistics, by 2029.

materials-perovskite-primary-power.title: Perovskite arrays power operational satellites
materials-perovskite-primary-power.description: Perovskite-based (tandem or thin-film) arrays serve as primary power on operational spacecraft, for example lightweight arrays for compute or broadband constellations.
materials-perovskite-primary-power.status_oct2026: Not operational anywhere as of Oct 2026 (general); flight experiments only.
materials-perovskite-primary-power.why: In 33FG's orbital-compute model, thin-film arrays (~1.7 kW/kg) versus rigid arrays (~0.8 kW/kg) roughly halve the Starship launches needed per 100 GW/yr of orbital compute (~600 versus ~1,200). One to two years of on-orbit lifetime evidence gate adoption; risk-tolerant constellation operators with five-year design lives adopt first.
materials-perovskite-primary-power.strongest_case_small: Thin-film CIGS, thinned III-V cells and better array structures may deliver the specific-power gain without perovskites, and falling launch costs reduce the value of mass savings.
materials-perovskite-primary-power.signpost: A constellation operator announces perovskite-based primary arrays on a production satellite batch, by 2030.

materials-in-space-mfg-product.title: Products made in orbit sold at recurring volume
materials-in-space-mfg-product.description: In-space-manufactured semiconductor substrates or crystals, or ZBLAN fiber, sold commercially at recurring volume, with quality advantages predicted by validated models.
materials-in-space-mfg-product.status_oct2026: Demonstrations only: ~12 km of ZBLAN on the ISS (2024), ForgeStar-1 plasma operations (from Dec 2025, deorbit planned 2026), Varda defense and pharmaceutical reentries (W-5, W-6 in 2026).
materials-in-space-mfg-product.why: Models tell investors which products clear the cost of launch and return, but recurring volume needs dedicated free-flyers, frequent return capsules and committed buyers, all physical and capital gates that AI cognition does not compress.
materials-in-space-mfg-product.strongest_case_small: Economics, not physics knowledge, binds, and terrestrial process improvements may close the quality gap.
materials-in-space-mfg-product.signpost: A multi-year offtake contract for orbit-made substrates or fiber with published quality metrics, by 2029.

materials-hot-section-reuse.title: Longer-life reusable engines from new alloys
materials-hot-section-reuse.description: Operational reusable engines whose hot-section parts (preburners, turbines, chambers) use AI-designed alloys and model-backed life prediction, extending refurbishment intervals or allowing higher chamber pressure.
materials-hot-section-reuse.status_oct2026: Not started (general); depends on the first AI-designed alloy flight.
materials-hot-section-reuse.why: Hot-section refurbishment is a major reuse cost driver (general); doubling the life of the most-replaced parts would cut turnaround cost, but proving life needs fleet hours and post-flight tear-downs, a physical clock.
materials-hot-section-reuse.strongest_case_small: Reuse economics are dominated by vehicle-level design and operations, and engine makers already iterate in-house alloys empirically without AI.
materials-hot-section-reuse.signpost: An operator attributes a refurbishment-interval increase to a new hot-section alloy, by 2031.

materials-qual-cycle-compression.title: Space materials insertion drops below five years
materials-qual-cycle-compression.description: Concept-to-flight insertion of new space materials (alloys, TPS, PV) falls from the historical 10-20+ years to five years or less as an industry pattern, shown by at least three materials in 2027-2031.
materials-qual-cycle-compression.status_oct2026: Historically 10-20 years (Materials Genome Initiative), and more than 20 years and ~$400M for aerospace insertion; GE spent about two decades and over $1B on ceramic-matrix composites; Ferrium M54 (under six years) is the fast exception.
materials-qual-cycle-compression.why: Cognition is perhaps 20-30% of insertion time (Ferrium M54: under one of under six years went to design; assumption generalizing it). The rest is physical evidence. Compression beyond ~30% requires the evidence rules themselves to change (model-informed allowables, part-level digital-twin certification), which is why this outcome waits on regulators even under S3.
materials-qual-cycle-compression.strongest_case_small: Standards bodies and programs change slowly; a few fast commercial examples will not make an industry norm by 2031.
materials-qual-cycle-compression.signpost: A NASA-STD-6030 revision or MMPDS/CMH-17 policy that lets model-based evidence substitute for part of the test matrix, by 2028-29.

materials-specific-power-step.title: A step change in spacecraft power per kilogram
materials-specific-power-step.description: A fleet-level gain of 30% or more in power-system specific power (W/kg of arrays, storage and power electronics) on new spacecraft, attributable to new materials: perovskite or thin-film PV, high-voltage radiation-robust wide-bandgap electronics, higher-energy cells.
materials-specific-power-step.status_oct2026: Gains today come from array architecture (roll-out and flexible blankets) and cell-efficiency increments (general).
materials-specific-power-step.why: Power-system mass sets launch counts for orbital compute (33FG: compute satellites become power- and thermal-limited), so this is the materials outcome with the largest space-economics leverage. But each material leg needs multi-year flight evidence, so even S2 and S3 land after 2031.
materials-specific-power-step.strongest_case_small: Array architecture and launch-cost moves dwarf material gains in this window.
materials-specific-power-step.signpost: Spec sheets of new compute or broadband buses citing new-material arrays, electronics or cells, by 2031.

physclock-flight-test-cadence.title: Monthly flight testing of a fully reusable heavy launcher
physclock-flight-test-cadence.description: A new fully reusable heavy launcher (Starship V3) flies at least 12 integrated flights in one calendar year, so flight data rather than analysis sets the pace of learning. This is the data generator that reuse, life-prediction and certification-by-analysis nodes downstream need.
physclock-flight-test-cadence.status_oct2026: Starship has flown 14 integrated flights since Apr 2023: five in 2025 (intervals 48-90 days) and three in 2026 (Flight 12 May 22, Flight 13 Jul 24, Flight 14 Sep 28; 63-66 days apart) after a ~7-month gap for the V2-to-V3 change. Flight 14 was the first orbital flight and deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites. The FAA authorized up to 25 Starbase launches a year in 2025 (general); LC-39A's first Starship launch is targeted for around year-end in the best case (Mach33).
physclock-flight-test-cadence.why: Cadence is set by vehicle build and pad turnaround: about nine weeks per V3 loop with one active pad. A second Starbase pad, LC-39A and first reflights (expected early 2027) bring the interval to 3-4 weeks, giving 12 or more flights in 2027. AI barely changes this: Flight 12 went from Musk's 'about 6 weeks' (Jan 26 2026) to May 22, about 2.8 times the stated interval, because of hardware (a Starbase component failure in April, an engine-out in flight), not analysis.
physclock-flight-test-cadence.strongest_case_small: Both V3 boosters flown so far were lost in landing burns, and a pad-damaging failure (as New Glenn suffered on May 28 2026) costs 3-12 months. Only five of the 25 authorized Starbase flights flew in 2025.
physclock-flight-test-cadence.signpost: Starship flight count in 2027 (12 or more confirms); LC-39A debut by mid-2027; sustained intervals below 30 days.

physclock-regulator-ai-capacity.title: Regulators review with AI tools
physclock-regulator-ai-capacity.description: The FAA's Office of Commercial Space Transportation, the FCC, NASA safety boards and ESA reviewers use AI systems to re-run and check applicants' flight-safety analyses, environmental documents and safety cases, raising reviewer throughput 2-5x without changing the rules.
physclock-regulator-ai-capacity.status_oct2026: The FAA proposed electronic license submissions and four burden-reducing Part 450 changes on Oct 5 2026 and a waiver of 13 statutory requirements on Jul 30 2026 (Federal Register). The FCC voted on a 'Licensing Assembly Line' replacing Part 25 with Part 100 on Jul 22 2026, aiming to cut satellite licensing from years to months. No agency has announced AI-assisted technical review of launch licenses (general).
physclock-regulator-ai-capacity.why: Reviewer hours, not statute, set most of the time between a complete application and a decision (statutory limit 180 days, general). A reviewer who can re-run a debris-risk or overpressure analysis with an AI agent in hours instead of weeks moves the queue. Reform supplies the rules regardless of AI; AI capacity decides whether the reformed process is staffed at 300+ U.S. launches a year.
physclock-regulator-ai-capacity.strongest_case_small: Agencies adopt slowly under procurement, FedRAMP, ITAR and liability constraints; much review time is interagency consultation, public comment and policy judgment that AI does not compress.
physclock-regulator-ai-capacity.signpost: FAA or FCC announcing AI-assisted review tooling; published median license evaluation times below 120 days.

physclock-optimal-test-campaigns.title: Tests chosen for information, not habit
physclock-optimal-test-campaigns.description: AI designs development and qualification test campaigns with Bayesian optimal experimental design and sequential testing, choosing which tests, levels, sensors and replicates buy the most margin knowledge. Typical test matrices shrink 20-40% and re-tests fall.
physclock-optimal-test-campaigns.status_oct2026: The methods exist (Bayesian experimental design, design of experiments, sequential probability-ratio tests) but are expert-scarce; space qualification follows enveloped levels and fixed matrices (GEVS, SMC-S-016, ECSS-E-ST-10-03, general). NASA's certification-by-analysis UQ discussion group published calibration and validation challenge problems (Jul 2025).
physclock-optimal-test-campaigns.premise_tier: n/a (capability premise); 139 is T3 but not load-bearing
physclock-optimal-test-campaigns.why: A 'solved in principle, expert-scarce' problem: on-demand applied math puts an experimental-design specialist on every campaign. Development tests, which operators control, change first; formal qualification follows customer acceptance. If test campaigns are ~25-35% of the critical path and AI trims 20-40% of test count, schedule gains are ~5-10% before any certification credit. Family 139 (subpolynomial-query log-concave sampling, T3) concerns the posterior sampling these designs use, but practical posteriors are already sampled adequately; it changes theory, not campaigns.
physclock-optimal-test-campaigns.strongest_case_small: Test count is driven by standards, customer requirements and workmanship screening, not information value; dropping a test that would have caught a workmanship error is a mission loss, so mission assurance will resist.
physclock-optimal-test-campaigns.signpost: A NASA, Space Force or prime-contractor test plan citing information-optimal design to cut a qualification matrix.

physclock-range-airspace-scheduling.title: Launch range and airspace scheduled by optimizer
physclock-range-airspace-scheduling.description: Range (Eastern, Western, Starbase) and national-airspace scheduling for hundreds to thousands of launches and reentries a year is done by optimization tools that minimize hazard-area closures and conflicts, so range time stops being a cadence limit.
physclock-range-airspace-scheduling.status_oct2026: U.S. orbital launches: 198 in 2025 and 140 by Oct 7 2026 (Wikipedia). Musk projects Starship launching 'more than once per hour' within 3-4 years (Jan 2026). Range and FAA airspace integration are coordinated largely by human schedulers (general).
physclock-range-airspace-scheduling.premise_tier: n/a; 124 is T1 (conditional) and not load-bearing
physclock-range-airspace-scheduling.why: Launch windows, hazard areas and range assets form a precedence-constrained scheduling problem that mixed-integer programming and heuristics already solve at today's scale; the gap is expert time and integration with FAA air-traffic systems. At 1,000+ flights a year from one coast it becomes a real constraint. Family 124 (polynomial-time scheduling on three identical machines, T1) is a theory result; its algorithm will not be what schedules ranges.
physclock-range-airspace-scheduling.strongest_case_small: Range capacity is limited by physical assets, safety buffers and airline-disruption politics, not schedule optimization; at 2026-2028 cadence the range is not the binding gate.
physclock-range-airspace-scheduling.signpost: FAA or Space Force announcing automated hazard-area and airspace scheduling; FAA-reported airspace delay minutes per launch falling.

physclock-credibility-evidence-standard.title: A rulebook for trusting AI-made analysis
physclock-credibility-evidence-standard.description: NASA-STD-7009, ECSS and Space Force test standards gain a defined way to count AI-generated analyses (with checked derivations, certified numerics and quantified model error) as verification evidence, with credibility levels that map to allowed test reductions.
physclock-credibility-evidence-standard.status_oct2026: NASA-STD-7009 sets model credibility. NASA's certification-by-analysis guide (May 2021) and UQ position paper (Jan 2024) place wide aircraft adoption in 2040-2050 and call tool credibility the open challenge; the NASA-FAA CM4QC strategy (Mar 2026) targets computational qualification of process-intensive metals. No standard addresses AI-generated analysis (general).
physclock-credibility-evidence-standard.why: Every test-substitution chain needs a rule saying what analysis evidence is worth. Standards bodies revise on 3-6 year cycles (general); S2's automated statement audits (2027) and verified numerics (2028) supply the evidence, so a first revision or NASA interim directive lands around 2029. Capped at Medium because it is regulator acceptance.
physclock-credibility-evidence-standard.strongest_case_small: NASA's own roadmap puts certification by analysis at 2040-2050 for aircraft; standards follow experience and accidents, not capability; a single failure traced to AI analysis would freeze adoption.
physclock-credibility-evidence-standard.signpost: A NASA-STD-7009 revision, NASA engineering directive or ECSS handbook naming AI-generated analysis; a CM4QC pilot granting qualification credit.

physclock-ai-mishap-analysis.title: Root cause in days, not months
physclock-ai-mishap-analysis.description: AI agents do the cognitive part of anomaly investigations (telemetry forensics, fault-tree pruning, physics re-simulation of candidate causes, corrective-action analysis), so return to flight is set by hardware fixes and verification tests rather than diagnosis.
physclock-ai-mishap-analysis.status_oct2026: Falcon 9 returned to flight 5 days after the Feb 1 2026 upper-stage deorbit-burn anomaly, with the FAA accepting SpaceX's findings (33FG). Starship loops in 2025 stretched to 82-90 days after the Flight 8 and 9 losses. New Glenn was grounded after an Apr 2026 upper-stage failure, and a May 28 2026 static-fire explosion destroyed a vehicle and damaged its pad (Wikipedia). The FAA accepts operator-led investigations (general).
physclock-ai-mishap-analysis.why: Diagnosis is cognitive and sits on the critical path: when the cause is clear, return to flight takes days (Falcon 9, Feb 2026); when it is ambiguous, weeks to months. Searching the cause space 5-10x faster cuts the diagnosis share (illustratively 30-60% of a 60-90 day investigation, general) to days; redesign, requalification tests and FAA acceptance remain. No new regulator acceptance is needed: the FAA reviews findings, not the tools used to reach them.
physclock-ai-mishap-analysis.strongest_case_small: The slow investigations are slow because hardware must be redesigned, rebuilt and retested or a pad rebuilt (New Glenn), none of which AI compresses; SpaceX already closes clear anomalies in under a week.
physclock-ai-mishap-analysis.signpost: An operator stating that AI tooling found a root cause; falling median time from mishap to FAA return-to-flight determination.

physclock-ai-flight-safety-analysis.title: License analyses drafted and checked by AI
physclock-ai-flight-safety-analysis.description: AI agents produce and cross-check the Part 450 flight-safety analysis (debris, far-field overpressure, toxic release, expected casualty), the ground-safety analysis and the NEPA environmental documents that operators submit, turning months of specialist effort into days.
physclock-ai-flight-safety-analysis.status_oct2026: The FAA proposed (Oct 5 2026) consolidating flight-safety-analysis information requirements, dropping overpressure analysis for hypothetical public locations and simplifying containment; Advisory Circular 413.13-1A (Jul 2026) revised application guidance. Specialist consultancies and in-house teams prepare these analyses today (general).
physclock-ai-flight-safety-analysis.why: These analyses use established methods (Monte Carlo debris dispersion, blast propagation, plume dispersion): expert-scarce, not research-hard. An AI running FAA-accepted methods needs no new acceptance; the FAA evaluates the outputs as it does today. Payoff: license modifications for new trajectories or cadence (for example New Glenn's 12-to-50-per-year review) are prepared in weeks.
physclock-ai-flight-safety-analysis.strongest_case_small: Preparation is rarely the long pole for an experienced operator; the long poles are environmental consultations, public comment and interagency review.
physclock-ai-flight-safety-analysis.signpost: An operator or consultancy publicly using AI-generated Part 450 analyses; shorter time from application to license modification.

physclock-qual-by-analysis-credit.title: Certification by analysis accepted for space hardware
physclock-qual-by-analysis-credit.description: NASA, Space Force and ESA mission-assurance practice grants formal test credit to validated analysis for derivative and similar hardware across structures, thermal, propulsion and avionics: protoflight instead of dedicated qualification units, reduced environmental levels, analysis-only delta qualification.
physclock-qual-by-analysis-credit.status_oct2026: Qualification by similarity and protoflight approaches exist for heritage hardware (general). NASA's aircraft certification-by-analysis roadmap targets 2040-2050; NASA-FAA CM4QC (Mar 2026) addresses additively manufactured metals; the structures domain places structural certification by analysis at 2030 in S2.
physclock-qual-by-analysis-credit.why: A dedicated qualification unit and campaign for a major subsystem costs months and often tens of millions of dollars (general). If AI-supplied credibility evidence lets derivative hardware skip qualification units, a typical derivative subsystem saves 6-12 months. First credit comes on derivatives and uncrewed missions where the customer owns the risk. Capped at Medium.
physclock-qual-by-analysis-credit.strongest_case_small: Tests find workmanship and integration errors that analysis cannot; first-of-kind and crewed hardware will keep full programs; commercial operators already skip tests where they own the risk, so the gain is mainly on government programs.
physclock-qual-by-analysis-credit.signpost: A NASA or Space Force program formally dropping a planned qualification test on the strength of AI-produced analysis.

physclock-ai-run-test-stands.title: Test stands that run themselves
physclock-ai-run-test-stands.description: Engine stands, thermal-vacuum chambers, vibration tables and materials rigs run around the clock under AI control with adaptive test sequences and automatic data reduction, raising facility utilization from roughly 30-50% to 70% or more and cutting test-to-insight time from weeks to hours.
physclock-ai-run-test-stands.status_oct2026: Autonomous laboratories exist for materials chemistry (DOE Genesis Mission first awards Jul 2026, per the capability domain); large aerospace test facilities run human-scheduled campaigns (general). The scarcest facilities are arc jets, large thermal-vacuum chambers and nuclear test infrastructure (general).
physclock-ai-run-test-stands.why: Test facilities are the scarcest physical asset; doubling utilization is worth a second facility (2-4 years and tens to hundreds of millions of dollars to build, general). Adaptive sequencing (stop when the information is in) and instant data reduction compress campaign calendar time 20-40% without new physics.
physclock-ai-run-test-stands.strongest_case_small: Utilization is limited by article build, setup, safety and consumables (propellant, liquid nitrogen), not scheduling; thermal soaks and life tests run in physical time.
physclock-ai-run-test-stands.signpost: A propulsion or test-services company reporting autonomous around-the-clock test operations with utilization figures.

physclock-nuclear-safety-case-ai.title: Nuclear launch safety cases in months
physclock-nuclear-safety-case-ai.description: AI produces the reactor design analyses (neutronics, thermal-hydraulics, accident criticality) and the launch-accident nuclear safety analysis needed for presidential-level launch approval of a space fission reactor, cutting a multi-year analysis cycle to months.
physclock-nuclear-safety-case-ai.status_oct2026: DRACO (nuclear thermal demo, Lockheed-BWXT contract Jul 2023 for a 2027 flight) was put on hold in Jan 2025 and cancelled in 2025, with DARPA citing falling launch costs. NASA unveiled Space Reactor-1 Freedom (over 20 kWe, nuclear-electric, two Mars flybys) in Mar 2026 for a Dec 2028 launch; its estimate reached $2.1B by Sep 2026 while Congress directed $10M to it in May 2026 (Wikipedia). Launch approval follows NSPM-20 (2019, general).
physclock-nuclear-safety-case-ai.why: Nuclear safety analysis is labor-dominated and export-controlled; on-demand applied math inside controlled networks compresses it from years to months. Interagency review and presidential approval remain, so capped at Medium.
physclock-nuclear-safety-case-ai.strongest_case_small: Space reactor programs die of funding and politics (SP-100, Prometheus, DRACO), not analysis; HALEU fuel and fabrication bind.
physclock-nuclear-safety-case-ai.signpost: A completed SR-1 Freedom safety analysis report and an FY2027 appropriation of several hundred million dollars.

physclock-starship-full-reuse.title: Both Starship stages caught and reflown
physclock-starship-full-reuse.description: A Starship V3 booster and ship are each recovered and flown again, the threshold that turns a $200-250M expendable stack into an amortizable fleet.
physclock-starship-full-reuse.status_oct2026: Booster catches were demonstrated with V2 (2024-25); both V3 boosters flown so far failed in landing burns (Flights 12 and 13); Flight 14 expended both stages by plan. Musk: Flight 15 attempts the first ship catch with odds of 'at least 50 or 60 percent', and ship and booster refly 'at the end of this year or more likely early next' (Mach33, Sep 2026).
physclock-starship-full-reuse.why: Reuse is a flight-test result. Falcon 9 took 15 months from first landing (Dec 2015) to first reflight (Mar 2017). AI shortens failure analysis between attempts but does not change the number of attempts needed.
physclock-starship-full-reuse.strongest_case_small: Ship catch and heat-shield refurbishment are unproven; repeated failures could push ship reflight into 2028 (Mach33 bear case).
physclock-starship-full-reuse.signpost: Flight 15 ship catch (about Dec 2026); first reflight of a caught booster and ship by mid-2027.

physclock-twin-reflight-clearance.title: Reflight cleared by data, not teardown
physclock-twin-reflight-clearance.description: Reusable stages are cleared for reflight from flight sensor data and a probabilistic life model (a digital twin) instead of detailed inspection, enabling booster turnaround under a week and ship turnaround under two weeks.
physclock-twin-reflight-clearance.status_oct2026: Falcon 9 in 2025: 95% of launches on reused boosters, median booster on its 14th flight, 38-day median turnaround, 162 missions from 25 airframes; cohort lifetimes rose from 4.2 flights (2018 boosters) to 8.0 (2019) and 24 (2020) (Mach33). No Starship stage has reflown.
physclock-twin-reflight-clearance.premise_tier: n/a (capability premise); 372 is T1 (conditional) and not load-bearing
physclock-twin-reflight-clearance.why: Mach33's base case has flights per stack at 3.3 (2027), 4.8 (2028), 8.9 (2029) and 18 (2030). Model-based clearance that pulls this curve forward 6-12 months is worth roughly $1-2B on the 2028 Starlink manifest alone (Mach33's 2028 base-to-bull spread is $1.6B). Life data still accrue one flight at a time. Family 372 (Lame moduli uniquely determined from boundary data, smooth isotropic case, T1) supports identifiability for inverse inspection in principle; damaged composites and welds lie outside its hypotheses.
physclock-twin-reflight-clearance.strongest_case_small: SpaceX scaled Falcon reuse through fleet-leader experience and inspection without formal twins; the limit is wear mechanisms (heat-shield tiles, engines) that only flights reveal.
physclock-twin-reflight-clearance.signpost: Starship booster turnaround under 7 days; SpaceX disclosing sensor-based reflight clearance.

physclock-reactor-in-space.title: A U.S. fission reactor launched
physclock-reactor-in-space.description: The first U.S. space fission reactor since SNAP-10A (1965) is launched: Space Reactor-1 Freedom (nuclear-electric, over 20 kWe) or a Fission Surface Power / Lunar Reactor-1 unit.
physclock-reactor-in-space.status_oct2026: SR-1 Freedom targets Dec 2028 at a $2.1B estimate with $10M directed (Wikipedia); Fission Surface Power had three Phase 1 teams from 2022 (Lockheed Martin, Westinghouse, IX), a 2025 executive order prioritizing a lunar reactor, and a directive targeting launch readiness around 2030; NASA said in Mar 2026 that SR-1 data will inform Lunar Reactor-1 (Wikipedia).
physclock-reactor-in-space.why: HALEU fuel supply, reactor fabrication, zero-power criticality testing and integration take roughly 4-6 years from a funded start (general). SR-1 is underfunded for Dec 2028; a 2029-30 launch needs FY2027-28 appropriations. AI shortens analysis and the safety case, worth perhaps 6-12 months.
physclock-reactor-in-space.strongest_case_small: Every U.S. space reactor program since 1965 has been cancelled; cheap launch removed DRACO's rationale; the 2026 cancellations of Gateway and Mars Sample Return show how fast NASA priorities shift.
physclock-reactor-in-space.signpost: FY2027 appropriation for SR-1; DOE fuel delivery; a reactor criticality test.

physclock-pad-propellant-infra.title: Pads and propellant plants for hundreds of heavy flights
physclock-pad-propellant-infra.description: At least four Starship-capable pads operate (Starbase pads 1 and 2, LC-39A, SLC-37 or equivalent) with on-site or pipeline propellant supply, removing pad count and cryogen trucking as cadence limits.
physclock-pad-propellant-infra.status_oct2026: Starbase has two pads; LC-39A's Starship debut is targeted around year-end at best (Mach33). A Starbase methane pipeline ('Starpipe') targets Jan 2027 service; SpaceX filed for a 32.4-mile Florida gas pipeline (Oct 2026); a $100B Louisiana campus (five complexes, two pads each) plans construction from 2027 and first launches as soon as 2029. Merchant supply needs about 389 tanker deliveries per flight (Mach33).
physclock-pad-propellant-infra.why: Pad construction (2-4 years per heavy pad, general) and air-separation and liquefaction plants run on the physical clock. On-site propellant costs about $0.2M per flight against $1.7-2.7M merchant, and trucking becomes physically implausible above about 100 flights a year (106 deliveries a day) (Mach33). AI barely touches this; it bounds every high-cadence node.
physclock-pad-propellant-infra.strongest_case_small: Environmental reviews, litigation or a pad-destroying failure can delay a site by a year or more; SpaceX may run fewer pads harder.
physclock-pad-propellant-infra.signpost: LC-39A's first Starship launch; Starpipe in service; Florida Public Service Commission approval of the pipeline.

physclock-heavy-cadence-100.title: 100+ fully reusable heavy launches a year
physclock-heavy-cadence-100.description: Fully reusable heavy launchers fly 100 or more orbital missions in one calendar year.
physclock-heavy-cadence-100.status_oct2026: 2025: 330 orbital launches worldwide, 165 by Falcon 9 (no failures), 5 by Starship; 2026 to Oct 7: 237 launches, 113 by Falcon 9, 3 by Starship (Wikipedia). Mach33's reference case has about 90 Starship flights carrying 10,100 t of Starlink in 2028; Musk says 'more than once per hour' within 3-4 years (Jan 2026).
physclock-heavy-cadence-100.why: At Mach33's 2028 base of 4.8 flights per stack, 100 flights need about 21 new stacks (roughly $3B at $143M each) and four or more pads; at 2030's 18 flights per stack, about 6 stacks. Production, reuse reliability and propellant bind. In S2 and S3, AI-run factories and faster anomaly closure add 6-12 months; S1 reaches it about 2030 on SpaceX's own trajectory.
physclock-heavy-cadence-100.strongest_case_small: Falcon 9 took from 2010 to 2022 to exceed 60 launches a year (general); each Starship failure grounds the fleet for weeks to months.
physclock-heavy-cadence-100.signpost: Starship flights in 2027 and 2028 (30 or more in 2028 keeps S2 on track); disclosed flights per stack.

physclock-reusable-competition.title: A second reusable heavy-lift fleet at scale
physclock-reusable-competition.description: A non-SpaceX reusable medium or heavy launcher fleet (New Glenn, Neutron, Terran R, Long March 10B, Zhuque-3 or another) flies 20 or more missions with reflown boosters in one calendar year.
physclock-reusable-competition.status_oct2026: New Glenn: announced 2016 for 2020, first flight Jan 16 2025, first booster landing Nov 13 2025, upper-stage failure Apr 19 2026, vehicle destroyed and pad damaged in a May 28 2026 static-fire explosion; the FAA's draft assessment would raise its cap from 12 to 50 a year (Sep 2026). Neutron: announced Mar 2021 for 2024-25, now NET Q4 2026. Terran R NET 2026. China recovered a Long March 10B booster after orbital flight on Jul 10 2026 (Wikipedia; 33FG).
physclock-reusable-competition.why: Mach33 modeled 15-36 New Glenn launches over 2026-27 and found cadence gated by BE-4 and upper-stage production, not reuse; every competitor slipped 1-5 years against announced first flights. AI helps new entrants most (no legacy process) but cannot shorten engine qualification or pad rebuilds.
physclock-reusable-competition.strongest_case_small: For U.S. customer prices only Western competition counts (export control, national-security rules); Chinese fleets do not lower U.S. prices.
physclock-reusable-competition.signpost: New Glenn return to flight and reflown-booster count; Neutron's first flight; Chinese reusable cadence in 2027.

physclock-licensing-in-weeks.title: Launch licensing in weeks
physclock-licensing-in-weeks.description: Routine license modifications (new trajectory, cadence or payload class) clear in under 30 days, new vehicle operator licenses in under six months from a complete application, and FCC satellite approvals in months.
physclock-licensing-in-weeks.status_oct2026: EO 14335 (Aug 2025) ordered Part 450 reform and NEPA streamlining; FAA proposed rules on Jul 30 and Oct 5 2026 waive statutory requirements and cut analysis burdens; the FCC adopted a Part 100 'Licensing Assembly Line' (vote Jul 22 2026). The statutory review clock for a complete application is 180 days (general).
physclock-licensing-in-weeks.why: Reform supplies the rules (final rules plausibly 2027-28); AI on both sides supplies the capacity. Together they turn licensing from a 6-18 month item into weeks for incremental changes. Capped at Medium because it is regulator behavior.
physclock-licensing-in-weeks.strongest_case_small: Licensing was not the binding gate for SpaceX in 2025-26 (hardware was); NEPA litigation and environmental consultations remain; a public-safety incident would reverse reform.
physclock-licensing-in-weeks.signpost: FAA final rules on the 2026 proposals; published license evaluation times; Starship license modifications approved without delaying flights.

physclock-critical-payload-reuse-accepta.title: Crew and national-security missions on data-cleared reused hardware
physclock-critical-payload-reuse-accepta.description: NASA crew or mission-critical payloads, or Space Force national-security missions, fly on reflown Starship-class hardware whose reflight clearance rests largely on flight data and life models rather than teardown inspection.
physclock-critical-payload-reuse-accepta.status_oct2026: Falcon 9 analog: first booster reflight Mar 2017; NASA crew on a reused booster with Crew-2 in Apr 2021, about four years later (general). HLS was not human-rated as of Apr 2026; Artemis III became a low-Earth-orbit test (NET Jun 2027) and the first landing moved to Artemis IV in early 2028 (Wikipedia).
physclock-critical-payload-reuse-accepta.why: The four-year Falcon lag was mostly evidence accumulation and customer process. AI-produced credibility evidence (standard in S2 around 2029) can cut it to two or three years after the first Starship reflight (2027). Capped at Medium because it is customer certification.
physclock-critical-payload-reuse-accepta.strongest_case_small: NASA crew safety posture will require flight history, not models; HLS and national-security missions may use new vehicles anyway, making the question moot before 2031.
physclock-critical-payload-reuse-accepta.signpost: NASA or Space Force accepting a reflown Starship for a mission; a NASA certification baseline for Starship reuse.

physclock-cheap-mass-internal.title: Starship internal cost under $300 per kg
physclock-cheap-mass-internal.description: SpaceX's internal cost to put a kilogram in low orbit on Starship falls below $300/kg, against about $1,500/kg on an optimized Falcon 9 Starlink flight and about $4,915/kg on expended Flight 14.
physclock-cheap-mass-internal.status_oct2026: Mach33 Launch Keystone v1.3 (Sep 2026): Flight 14 about $4,915/kg ($250M stack, 52 t); base $656/kg in 2027 and about $300/kg in 2028 (bear about $560, bull $141); $13/kg by 2035. Falcon 9 optimized Starlink flight about $1,499/kg at a $25M internal cost.
physclock-cheap-mass-internal.why: Mach33 splits the 2026-27 decline (log basis) into reuse 56%, payload 32% and production learning 12%. None is a mathematics lever. This is the independent physical exponential in this tree: it would happen at the same pace with no AI math at all.
physclock-cheap-mass-internal.strongest_case_small: Internal cost matters only to SpaceX's own payloads (Starlink, orbital compute); outside customers see prices, not costs (see physclock-cheap-mass-customer).
physclock-cheap-mass-internal.signpost: Flights per stack in 2027; payload per flight approaching 100 t.

physclock-cheap-mass-customer.title: Customers buy orbit under $1,000 per kg
physclock-cheap-mass-customer.description: Third-party customers can routinely buy dedicated heavy-lift capacity below $1,000/kg, against a Falcon 9 dedicated median of about $5,300/kg and a rideshare floor of about $7,000/kg today.
physclock-cheap-mass-customer.status_oct2026: Mach33 Launch Unlock model (Aug 2026): Starship third-party ticket enters at about $3,975/kg in 2027 and fades toward cost with a 2033 midpoint (2030-36 range) as competitors reach cadence; Voyager's $90M Starlab contract implies about $900/kg for a 2028-29 launch. SpaceX flew 83% of 2025 mass to orbit.
physclock-cheap-mass-customer.why: Price follows competition, not cost: Falcon 9 list prices were stable for a decade, and Mach33 finds a one-year delay in credible competitor cadence delays external crossover by about a year. AI math reaches this node only by speeding competitors' engineering.
physclock-cheap-mass-customer.strongest_case_small: Anchor deals like Voyager's already price near $900/kg, so 'routine' is a soft threshold; the markets most sensitive to $/kg (Starlink, orbital compute) are SpaceX's own and see internal cost.
physclock-cheap-mass-customer.signpost: Published Starship rideshare or dedicated pricing; a second Starship-class customer contract below $1,500/kg.

physclock-qual-cycle-compressed.title: Qualification cycles 30-50% shorter
physclock-qual-cycle-compressed.description: Typical qualification of a new or derivative spacecraft or launch-vehicle subsystem falls from roughly 12-24 months to 8-14 months through fewer, better-chosen tests, analysis credit and autonomous facilities.
physclock-qual-cycle-compressed.status_oct2026: Qualification remains test-driven; NASA-STD-6030 requires per-machine qualification for additive parts; new space materials take 10-20+ years to insert (Materials Genome Initiative: 20 or more years from discovery to market).
physclock-qual-cycle-compressed.why: Composite: test count down 20-40% (optimal design), calendar time per test down 20-40% (autonomous stands), qualification units skipped for derivatives (analysis credit). The incompressible core is thermal-vacuum time constants, real-time life and creep tests (a 10,000-hour creep test takes about 14 months) and statistical replicates. Capped at Medium.
physclock-qual-cycle-compressed.strongest_case_small: Organizations spend saved time on more testing; first-of-kind hardware keeps full programs; the cut lands mostly on derivatives.
physclock-qual-cycle-compressed.signpost: GAO, ESA or company schedule data showing shorter qualification phases on programs started in 2028 or later.

physclock-test-loop-monthly.title: Monthly build-fly-fix loops on new heavy vehicles
physclock-test-loop-monthly.description: A new heavy-launch program sustains integrated flight tests at intervals of 30 days or less for six consecutive flights, with analysis and anomaly resolution no longer on the critical path.
physclock-test-loop-monthly.status_oct2026: Starship V3 intervals were 63-66 days in 2026 and V2 intervals 48-90 days in 2025; Flight 12 slipped from Musk's 'about 6 weeks' (Jan 26 2026) to May 22, about 17 weeks.
physclock-test-loop-monthly.why: Loop time is build plus test plus pad turnaround plus analysis. With two to four pads and reuse, build and turnaround fall under 30 days; AI removes most of the analysis share (illustratively 20-35% of a 60-day loop today, general). Learning rate then tracks physical throughput.
physclock-test-loop-monthly.strongest_case_small: SpaceX may reach 30-day intervals in 2027 on hardware alone; AI's contribution will be impossible to separate.
physclock-test-loop-monthly.signpost: Six consecutive Starship flights at intervals of 30 days or less.

physclock-dev-capital-cut.title: AI cuts development capital for new space hardware by 15-30%
physclock-dev-capital-cut.description: Non-recurring development cost for new spacecraft and launch vehicles falls 15-30% under S2 as engineering labor for analysis, design, software and verification shrinks; hardware, test articles and facilities do not shrink.
physclock-dev-capital-cut.status_oct2026: Starship program spend exceeded $15B by 2026, against roughly $400M for Falcon 9 development, and SpaceX directed all $3B of its 2025 space-segment R&D to Starship (Reuters via 33FG). SpaceX held $100.8B in cash after an $85.7B IPO in June 2026. Mach33 counts about $250M into orbital-compute hardware specialists since Jan 2025.
physclock-dev-capital-cut.why: Engineering labor is roughly 40-60% of space development cost (general); halving its analysis, design and software content cuts program cost 15-30%. That matters most for capital-gated new entrants; for SpaceX capital is not binding through 2031.
physclock-dev-capital-cut.strongest_case_small: Labor savings get spent on scope; hardware-rich programs like Starship spend mainly on hardware; government cost growth comes from requirements and funding instability.
physclock-dev-capital-cut.signpost: Startup raises and program estimates citing AI-reduced engineering headcount; NASA cost-estimating relationships revised for AI.

physclock-new-entrant-fast-orbit.title: A new reusable launcher from start to orbit in three years
physclock-new-entrant-fast-orbit.description: A program started in 2027 or later reaches orbit with a reusable medium or heavy launcher within three years of program start.
physclock-new-entrant-fast-orbit.status_oct2026: Historical: Falcon 9 about 5 years (2005-2010) and Electron about 5 years to orbit (2013-2018) (general); New Glenn announced 2016 for 2020 and flew Jan 2025; Neutron announced Mar 2021 and is NET Q4 2026; the BE-4 engine alone took from 2011 to first flight in Jan 2024 (Wikipedia).
physclock-new-entrant-fast-orbit.why: Even with cognitive work nearly free, engine development (hot-fire campaigns, turbopump failures), pad construction (2-4 years) and flight-test learning set a floor of about 4-5 years. AI's best case removes about a year, and only programs started after AI adoption (2027-28 in S2) benefit.
physclock-new-entrant-fast-orbit.strongest_case_small: This node is itself the small-effect case; the exception would be a derivative vehicle built around an existing engine.
physclock-new-entrant-fast-orbit.signpost: A 2027-28 program reaching full-scale hot fire within 12 months and pad readiness within 24.

physclock-satellite-gen-cadence.title: New satellite generations every year
physclock-satellite-gen-cadence.description: Leading commercial constellation operators field a new satellite generation (new bus or payload, not only software) about every 12 months, against 18-36 months today.
physclock-satellite-gen-cadence.status_oct2026: Starlink: v0.9 May 2019, v1.0 late 2019, v1.5 2021, v2 mini Feb 2023, v2 mini optimized (average satellite mass down from 623 kg to 575 kg, 96 Gbps), V3 (about 1 Tbps, about 2 t) first flown on Flight 13 (Jul 2026) and first orbited on Flight 14 (Sep 28 2026). V3's timing was gated by Starship, not the satellite. V2 mini production reached six a day by Mar 2023 (Wikipedia; Mach33).
physclock-satellite-gen-cadence.why: Design, software and verification compress in S2; payload qualification, radiation testing, line retooling and the launcher bind. Faster generations raise capacity per kilogram (V3 carries about three times V2 mini's capacity per kilogram, Mach33).
physclock-satellite-gen-cadence.strongest_case_small: Generation cadence is set by launcher steps and fleet economics (about five-year satellite life), not design speed; operators may prefer continuous incremental change.
physclock-satellite-gen-cadence.signpost: A Starlink V3.x or V4 announcement within 18 months of V3; Amazon Leo's second-generation timeline.

plasma-vm-wellposed.title: Plasma's master equation proved well-behaved (checked)
plasma-vm-wellposed.description: The claimed proof that the 3D relativistic Vlasov-Maxwell system (the kinetic equation for collisionless plasma coupled to Maxwell's equations) has global smooth solutions for smooth finite-energy data passes an outside Comparator run and a statement audit, moving from T3 to T4. This is the Glassey-Strauss global-regularity problem, open since the 1980s.
plasma-vm-wellposed.status_oct2026: Family 362 [L], T3: agent-written Lean main result in the repo, unchecked by outsiders as of 2026-10-07; no outside commentary on 362 found in search. Before the release, only continuation criteria (Glassey-Strauss 1986: smooth while momentum support stays bounded), small-data and symmetric results existed, e.g. vacuum stability for relativistic Vlasov-Maxwell-Boltzmann (Cao and Li, arXiv 2601.04018, Jan 2026).
plasma-vm-wellposed.why: The Lean proof exists, so a Comparator run is cheap; the slow part is the statement audit (does the Lean definition of the system, its function spaces and 'finite energy' match what physicists mean?). The March 2026 AI-assisted formalization of the Vlasov-Maxwell-Landau equilibrium reported exactly these definition-alignment bugs and hypothesis creep, which is why the gate is formalization rather than cognition. Hexagon (launched Oct 6, 2026) exists to do this. Once T4, every collisionless-plasma kinetic code is known to approximate a solution that exists and stays smooth for all time: a confidence gain, per analyst position (d).
plasma-vm-wellposed.strongest_case_small: Codes never waited for this; physicists assumed it. The theorem covers the whole-space relativistic system without walls, collisions or external circuits, while Hall-thruster, magnetic-nozzle and magnetosphere codes use electrostatic, non-relativistic, collisional or bounded-domain versions that are different equations. Nothing in a thruster, forecast or fusion device changes.
plasma-vm-wellposed.signpost: An outside Comparator report and statement audit for family 362 posted on Hexagon or by a kinetic-theory group within 12 months; a definition mismatch found in the audit would break this node and downgrade plasma-verified-kinetic-numerics.

plasma-landau-longtime.title: When do collisionless plasmas settle down? (Landau damping beyond idealized cases)
plasma-landau-longtime.description: Proofs of nonlinear Landau damping and long-time kinetic stability in physically realistic settings: finite (Sobolev) regularity, magnetized plasmas, bounded domains with absorbing or emitting walls, and electromagnetic fields. These say when and how fast kinetic fluctuations damp, which is what fluid closures try to imitate.
plasma-landau-longtime.status_oct2026: Open research problem, not in the openai/math catalog (closest: family 362, which is global existence, not decay). Nonlinear Landau damping is proved for Vlasov-Poisson with analytic or Gevrey data (Mouhot-Villani 2011) and is known to be delicate at finite regularity because of plasma echoes (general).
plasma-landau-longtime.why: The release shows the model settling decades-old kinetic-PDE problems at ~3 hours of compute per result; Landau-type questions are of comparable depth. Under S2, outside kinetic theorists get research-grade access in ~mid-2027 and can pose the realistic variants themselves (analyst position (a)); results arrive within months. The value is downstream: knowing which damping mechanisms survive nonlinearly and at what regularity tells closure builders (plasma-kinetic-closures) which Landau-fluid terms are legitimate.
plasma-landau-longtime.strongest_case_small: Linear Landau damping already works well in practice, and theorems for idealized geometries rarely change which closure an engineer picks. In Hall thrusters the hard physics is instability-driven turbulence, not the decay of smooth perturbations, so this may stay a mathematician's result.
plasma-landau-longtime.signpost: An AI-assisted preprint proving Landau damping for a magnetized or bounded-domain Vlasov system at Sobolev regularity, with a Lean statement, by end-2027.

plasma-lean-kinetic-library.title: A formal library for plasma equations
plasma-lean-kinetic-library.description: Agreed, reusable Lean definitions of Vlasov-Poisson/Maxwell, Landau and Boltzmann collision operators, ideal and Hall MHD, and their standard solution concepts, so any claimed result about a plasma model can be audited against a fixed statement.
plasma-lean-kinetic-library.status_oct2026: Mathlib coverage of PDE is thin (3 of 16 PDE families in the release have Lean). Proof of concept: one mathematician supervising Gemini DeepThink, Claude Code and Aristotle formalized the Vlasov-Maxwell-Landau equilibrium characterization in 10 days for about $200, writing no code (arXiv 2603.15929, Mar 2026).
plasma-lean-kinetic-library.why: Statement audits for 362, 363 and 364 and any future plasma theorem need shared definitions; the VML case shows the cost has fallen to days and hundreds of dollars, so the limit is agreeing on definitions, not writing proofs. Under S2, Mathlib analysis/PDE coverage catches up 2027-29 and a plasma layer follows within a year.
plasma-lean-kinetic-library.strongest_case_small: Engineering codes do not use Lean, and a definitions library mostly serves mathematicians. Matching a Lean object to the equation a physicist actually simulates still needs scarce human experts.
plasma-lean-kinetic-library.signpost: A Mathlib or Hexagon pull request adding standard definitions of the Vlasov-Maxwell system and its solution concepts, cited by a family-362 audit.

plasma-verified-kinetic-numerics.title: Plasma simulations with certified error bars
plasma-verified-kinetic-numerics.description: Convergence proofs and computable error bounds for structure-preserving Vlasov-Maxwell, particle-in-cell (PIC) and MHD discretizations, increasingly machine-checked, so code verification can state 'discretization error below X' instead of relying on convergence studies.
plasma-verified-kinetic-numerics.status_oct2026: Structure-preserving (geometric) PIC and finite-element schemes exist with proved conservation properties (general); convergence theorems typically assume a smooth solution exists on the time interval, an assumption family 362 [L, T3] removes for relativistic Vlasov-Maxwell. PIC statistical noise and the electron-to-xenon mass ratio of about 1:239,000 (stiffness) lack rigorous error control (general).
plasma-verified-kinetic-numerics.why: Under S2, AI does numerics with certified error bounds by 2027-28 and the verified floating-point toolchain matures 2027-29, so the first certified kinetic-solver modules appear ~2029. Practical value: replacing grid- and particle-count convergence studies (often several times the cost of the production run, general) with proof-backed estimators, and giving ML surrogates a certified reference to be checked against.
plasma-verified-kinetic-numerics.strongest_case_small: Turbulent plasma simulations are chaotic, so rigorous long-time error bounds grow with the Lyapunov time and can be valid but useless for the time-averaged transport engineers want. Model-form error (closures, wall physics) dwarfs discretization error in Hall-thruster and space-weather codes.
plasma-verified-kinetic-numerics.signpost: A plasma code team (e.g. WarpX, GEMPIC, GX) ships a module with a machine-checked convergence or conservation proof and uses it in a V&V report.

plasma-kinetic-solvers-at-scale.title: Full-thruster kinetic simulation becomes affordable
plasma-kinetic-solvers-at-scale.description: AI-designed algorithms (implicit and asymptotic-preserving PIC, low-rank and sparse-grid Vlasov solvers, bounded learned subgrid models) make 3D whole-device kinetic simulation of a Hall thruster with real mass ratio, real geometry and wall physics a days-long rather than infeasible calculation.
plasma-kinetic-solvers-at-scale.status_oct2026: Facility-scale kinetic simulations of Hall thrusters do not yet exist at feasible cost (Whittaker, Marks, Gorodetsky, AIAA 2026). 3D PIC with wall charging, secondary emission and near-plume outflow (Liu, Zhao, Zhao, arXiv 2603.14849, Mar 2026) shows anomalous transport self-organizing into near-wall pathways, but at reduced scale. In fusion, GPU-native gyrokinetics (GX) already runs useful turbulence cases in minutes on one GPU.
plasma-kinetic-solvers-at-scale.why: Algorithm invention for multiscale kinetic problems is expert-scarce work that S2 makes on-demand by 2027-28. Historical algorithmic gains in kinetic simulation (implicit, energy-conserving PIC) were 10-100x (general); stacking another 10-100x from AI-designed methods on exascale GPUs plausibly gets whole-device runs. This is the enabling step for both the anomalous-transport closure and design-before-build thrusters.
plasma-kinetic-solvers-at-scale.strongest_case_small: The problem spans six-plus orders of magnitude in time scale; some cost may be irreducible and algorithm gains could stall near 10x. Even perfect kinetic simulations inherit uncertain wall, secondary-emission and facility-pressure physics, so cheaper runs do not automatically remove uncertainty.
plasma-kinetic-solvers-at-scale.signpost: A published full-device 3D PIC of a >=5 kW Hall thruster at real mass ratio, run in under a week, reproducing measured discharge current within 10% with no tuned anomalous coefficients.

plasma-gk-surrogates.title: Millisecond fusion-turbulence models trusted in design
plasma-gk-surrogates.description: Neural and quasilinear surrogates of gyrokinetic turbulence that run in milliseconds, carry calibrated uncertainty, and are trusted inside reactor-design and scenario-planning loops in place of hours-to-weeks nonlinear simulations.
plasma-gk-surrogates.status_oct2026: Already arriving through ML, not frontier math: surrogates of the GX code trained on >200,000 nonlinear simulations over ~23,000 stellarator configurations run in ~ms and are used directly in equilibrium optimization (Churchill, Landreman et al., arXiv 2609.28730, Sep 23 2026); GyroSwin cuts fully resolved nonlinear gyrokinetics cost ~1,000x (arXiv 2510.07314); PQLS calibrates a quasilinear saturation rule by Bayesian inference, separating parameter and model-form uncertainty (arXiv 2609.29336, Sep 24 2026). Multiscale nonlinear runs can cost ~640,000 node-hours (search summary of GKV on Fugaku).
plasma-gk-surrogates.why: The training data and ML methods exist; DOE's Genesis Mission/STELLAR-AI (PPPL, Jan 2026) funds exactly this. AI applied math adds out-of-distribution error bounds and principled UQ on top, raising trust from 'useful screening tool' to 'design-of-record input'.
plasma-gk-surrogates.strongest_case_small: This is ML engineering already underway, so the AI-math increment is small. Surrogates trained on adiabatic-electron simulations miss kinetic-electron and electromagnetic effects that matter at reactor-relevant pressure, so trust may stay limited to early design.
plasma-gk-surrogates.signpost: A fusion company publishes a design whose surrogate-predicted transport is later confirmed within its stated error bars by experiment (W7-X or a new device).

plasma-swx-data-assimilation.title: Sun-to-Earth ensemble forecasting with honest uncertainty
plasma-swx-data-assimilation.description: Coupled data assimilation from the Sun (SDO imagery and magnetograms, coronagraphs) through the solar wind (SOLAR-1 at L1) to the magnetosphere, ionosphere and thermosphere, producing ensemble forecasts with calibrated probabilities rather than single deterministic runs.
plasma-swx-data-assimilation.status_oct2026: SOLAR-1 (ex-SWFO-L1) launched Sep 24, 2025 and reached L1 Jan 23, 2026. NOAA's WAM-IPE gives 2-day ionosphere-thermosphere forecasts (operational since July 2021, upgraded 2023). NASA/IBM's open Surya heliophysics foundation model (Aug 2025, 360M parameters, 9 years of SDO data) beats flare benchmarks by ~16% up to 2 h ahead. Density models rarely propagate uncertainty to orbit decisions (CPAESS 2026 workshop abstract).
plasma-swx-data-assimilation.why: Ensemble data assimilation for a nonlinear, sparsely observed coupled system (filter design, model-error estimation, localization, feature alignment of CME fronts) is bespoke, expert-scarce applied math; S2 makes it on-demand by 2027-28. Terrestrial weather shows what DA buys: roughly a day of useful lead time per decade (general).
plasma-swx-data-assimilation.strongest_case_small: Space weather is observation-starved: one L1 point, a few coronagraph viewpoints and no routine coronal magnetic-field measurement. Assimilation cannot create information that is not observed; Kay et al. (2024) attribute CME arrival-time errors mainly to input reconstruction and background solar wind.
plasma-swx-data-assimilation.signpost: SWPC or ESA's space-weather service transitions an assimilative ensemble heliospheric model to operations with published reliability diagrams by 2028.

plasma-kinetic-closures.title: Fluid plasma models derived from kinetic theory, with error bounds
plasma-kinetic-closures.description: Physics theory that derives fluid closures (electron heat flux, anomalous resistivity, pressure anisotropy, Landau-fluid terms) from kinetic theory with stated validity domains and error bounds, replacing ad hoc closures in thruster, magnetic-nozzle and magnetospheric fluid codes.
plasma-kinetic-closures.status_oct2026: Engineering plasma codes are fluid or hybrid with hand-tuned closures; magnetic-nozzle expansion is nearly collisionless and needs a non-trivial electron closure (Kim et al., PSST 2023). No catalog family addresses closures. Family 364 (Boltzmann derived from Newtonian gases, with fluctuations over the Boltzmann lifespan; T1, conditional) is a step in the same particles-to-kinetic-to-fluid derivation program, methodological relevance only.
plasma-kinetic-closures.premise_tier: n/a (364 is T1 and not load-bearing)
plasma-kinetic-closures.why: S2 assumes AI builds and validates physics theory and reduced models from 2028-29; closures are the canonical such task. Validation needs kinetic simulation data (plasma-kinetic-solvers-at-scale) and diagnostics such as incoherent Thomson scattering, which already exist at university labs.
plasma-kinetic-closures.strongest_case_small: Closures in turbulent, wall-bounded plasmas may not exist in closed form (they are non-local and history-dependent); the best achievable may be data-driven closures with UQ, which do not need frontier math.
plasma-kinetic-closures.signpost: A closure derived with AI assistance is adopted in a production code (HallThruster.jl, Hall2De, BATS-R-US) and cuts the number of calibrated parameters.

plasma-hall-anomalous-closure.title: Solving the 60-year Hall-thruster electron transport puzzle
plasma-hall-anomalous-closure.description: A validated, first-principles model of anomalous cross-field electron transport in Hall thrusters that predicts transport from the local plasma state across thrusters and operating points, without per-condition calibration.
plasma-hall-anomalous-closure.status_oct2026: Open research problem since the 1960s. Codes calibrate an anomalous collision frequency to each operating point. A self-consistent closure using plasma density, neutral density and electron temperature captures peak electron temperature and performance on a 9 kW magnetically shielded thruster but cannot place electron temperature and ion velocity profiles correctly at the same time (Brick, Roberts, Jorns, IEPC-2025-361).
